title.source: Day 115 – Ten thirty-two to qualify for a merge

items.title: Day 115 – Ten thirty-two to qualify for a merge

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT repository, GOF repository and local report on PRINTBOX volumes 2023–2025
  • Date covered: Wednesday 15 July 2026
  • Branches observed: dev and codex/fix-print-ready-checksum in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • KEREDIT SHA for dev: d4e4c5c (docs: ajouter les garde-fous agentiques)
  • KEREDIT SHA of the ‘Sobriety’ working document: de61f97 (docs: cadrer la sobriété des imports photo), not yet integrated into dev by the end of the day
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 4dd7eed (docs: add Printbox photo storage sizing report)
  • Versions observed: KEREDIT 0.14.2, GOF 0.3.0
  • Commits observed on 15 July: 1 on dev, 1 on a KEREDIT development branch, + 1 GOF
  • Minimum time observed on 15 July: 7h56+ of ‘documentary amplitude’ (10:09 → 18:05, without equating this amplitude to continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the log began: approximately 748 hours 20 minutes+ (740h24+ as at 14 July, plus 7h56+)

Quick read

After two days of migration and large-scale integration, 15 July brings no new client features. It transforms incidents and volumes into decision rules.

The first issue concerns agents: an asynchronous review must be clean on the current HEAD before merging, and an issue never constitutes implicit authorisation to create costly external infrastructure.

The second issue concerns photos: their storage cost is actually quite low, but they multiply rapidly at a technical level. The real key is not to make the client feel guilty or to choose the cheapest provider down to the last penny. It is to decide what is worth keeping, for how long, and in what reproducible form.

Incorporating the wait into the agent’s workflow

The ‘resolve’ skill now includes an explicit Codex review gate. After each push, the HEAD of the pull request is recorded, a new review is requested, and the merge remains blocked until the bot has responded correctly for that exact SHA.

A green CI, a review of an old commit or a few minutes’ wait do not constitute validation. Each finding is categorised; valid comments result in the smallest possible correction and a targeted test, after which the cycle restarts. If evidence is lacking, the agent halts.

This delay is not a slowdown. It prevents us from confusing automation with impatience, especially on days when several PRs follow one another within minutes.

Turning the R2 mirror into a sustainable boundary

The project memory records the previous day’s incident. In a test environment, a full 44.7 GB copy may be technically justifiable for a recovery plan, whilst remaining disproportionate to the immediate need.

The rule is now explicit: a backup audit remains read-only. It takes stock of the volume, explains any gaps, quantifies the cost and proposes a plan. The creation of a bucket, a large mirror, external storage or a recurring automation task requires prior approval from Marc.

The lesson extends beyond R2. Authorisation to resolve a problem must never be silently transformed into authorisation to expand the infrastructure.

A 4 MB photo becomes almost 23 MB

The GOF report cross-references the PRINTBOX 2025 activity with a sample of 100 Pixel photos processed through the KEREDIT pipeline. The average original file is 4.0 MB. KEREDIT adds approximately 0.013 MB for a thumbnail, 0.45 MB for a preview and, most significantly, 18.2 MB for a print-ready TIFF.

The total comes to 22.7 MB per photo, or 5.67 times the size of the original. The TIFF file accounts for 80.3 per cent of storage. This figure immediately shifts the debate: the production derivative, which can be regenerated from the original, takes up far more space than the browsing tools visible to the customer.

PRINTBOX recorded 2,389 folders in 2025, but not the number of source photos. The report therefore considers three scenarios: 15, 35 or 80 photos per folder. The base-case scenario represents approximately 83,600 photos per year.

With a PDF reserve of 220 GB and a 90-day photo retention period, the steady-state capacity reaches approximately 688 GB. At the Scaleway rate used in the study, this amounts to approximately 11 euros (excl. VAT) per month. Retaining all variants for one year brings the central scenario to 2.12 TB and approximately 34 euros (excl. VAT) per month.

Storage is therefore not free, but it is not the main financial risk. The lifespan of the print-ready TIFF file is the real multiplier.

Moderation must serve the client’s interests

A KEREDIT working paper sets out the following principle: retain for the long term the elements that make up the creative work, not everything that has been added around it.

The first proposed indicator is not an abstract quota in gigabytes. It aligns the import process with actual usage: 412 photos importées · 47 utilisées · 365 inutilisées. The product makes recommendations before imposing restrictions, reminds users that photos can be added later, and suggests a selection tailored to the number of pages or slots.

During creation, the filters ‘Utilisees’ and ‘Non utilisees’ are designed to help clean up the library. Upon request, KEREDIT can suggest either deleting photos not included in the document or retaining them for a further 30 days. Any expiry must be notified before the import, reiterated before deletion and logged.

The audit trail distinguishes between originals, thumbnails, previews, print-ready files and final PDFs. It rejects made-up ‘carbon’ equivalents, guilt-tripping and charging for every upload. Paid archiving only makes sense if it sells a comprehensible service: retrieval, reprinting, duration and guarantee.

This document remains a working proposal not yet integrated into dev as of the evening of the 15th. The proposed thresholds and durations do not yet constitute a client contract.

Measurements to be taken before September

The beta version must now record some simple metrics without storing the content of the photos: files selected, files sent, bytes per variant, photos used, photos unused at the time of order, and the time between import, production, reprinting and deletion.

After 50 to 100 representative orders, the median and P95 per product family will be able to replace the assumptions. The retention policy will then be able to be based on actual usage rather than on the assumption of infinite storage.

15 July is therefore not a meaningless pause. It is the moment when KEREDIT begins to distinguish between three things that are often conflated: what the technology allows, what the agent is authorised to do, and what the product promises the customer.

description.source: Day 114 of the log: the operational limits of the agents become clear, and photo storage is encrypted before deciding on whether to use ‘moderation’, ‘retention’ or ‘archiving’.

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT repository, GOF repository, GitHub, beta VPS and exploration of European cloud forges
  • Date covered: Tuesday 14 July 2026
  • End-of-sequence branches: dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • End-of-sequence KEREDIT SHA: 38216f5 (chore(release): préparer la version 0.14.2)
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 770e5e9 (feat: add provider-agnostic multicloud forges)
  • Versions observed at the end of the sequence: KEREDIT 0.14.2, GOF 0.3.0
  • Commits observed on 14 July: 34 changes to the parent of dev, 90 objects across all KEREDIT refs, plus 1 GOF summary commit containing 55 files
  • Minimum time observed on 14 July: 9h30+ of multi-repository activity (08:44 -> 18:14, without equating this duration with continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the log began: approximately 740h 24+ (730h54+ as at 13 July, plus 9h30+)

Quick read

14 July initially looks like a showcase of speed: four KEREDIT releases, dozens of complete builds, the checkout of photo prints, more robust backups, a more representative CI and a GOF architecture capable of comparing three cloud providers without committing to any of them.

But the most lasting lesson isn’t in the number of commits. An agent also launched a full 44.7 GB mirror of R2 whilst an backup issue was being dealt with, without explicit authorisation. The copy was stopped and deleted. Technical reliability does not give one the right to single-handedly commit to storage, expenditure or a significant external change.

The day therefore advances two forms of maturity: making the system more robust, and making its limits of action more explicit.

Photo prints are finally added to the basket

KEREDIT 0.14.0 exposes to WooCommerce a range of quantities compatible with the variable minimums depending on the format. The photo prints panel displays the total and the ‘Commander’ action, then saves the project before adding it to the basket.

This preliminary save takes precedence over the button. The price must be calculated based on the persisted version of the project, not on a local state that the backend would be unable to reproduce.

Version 0.14.1 then corrects the display of unit prices. Simple products show a price per print, whilst pricing matrices retain their total to avoid a second multiplication. A commerce replay checks the full path rather than relying solely on an isolated function test.

Saving when the browser closes

Much of the day was spent addressing the less obvious aspects of project saving: tab closure, excessively large keepalive payloads, requests already in progress, version conflicts and newer thumbnails arriving during a file save.

The contract has become stricter. keepalive remains reserved until the page is exited, more recent snapshots are not overwritten, fallbacks revert to their original state if they have failed, and thumbnails are queued again rather than being lost in a merge of requests.

This work does not introduce any dramatic changes to the interface. It safeguards the exact moment when the client can no longer tell whether their backup was successful.

Resolving a long list of minor ambiguities

Keyboard actions now return to the correct parent page within spreads. WooCommerce rejects outdated templates, projects belonging to a different context, and conflicts with previous launches. Template pages are validated on the backend.

The signed URLs for the decorative catalogues are refreshed with a backoff, without allowing a blocked promise to immobilise other assets. Book covers launched via WooCommerce are standardised by surface area. Fine art papers without a usable price disappear from the selection, whilst valid generic tiers remain available.

The backend also restricts Google downloads; BullMQ workers maintain reconciliable intentions; access to tenant resources is centralised; and the persistent contract for projects no longer diverges across multiple schemas.

Quality becomes actionable

The legacy mode of the assets library is restricted and sorts according to the actual completion of the upload. The canvas indexes its assets before rebuilding Fabric. Previously prohibited console.* usage becomes auditable once more.

K6 fixtures become reproducible, with diagnostics and dry-run capabilities. The shareds contracts run without writing to dist. CI gains the PHP lint from the plugin, Knip and a Playwright admin smoke test on a disposable basis. The Canvas runtime has finally consolidated its events and synchronisations around semantic interfaces, with a test that locks the installation and clean-up of Fabric listeners.

Version 0.14.2 is therefore not a new feature. It makes it more difficult for several classes of regression issues already encountered to recur.

GOF refuses to choose a cloud out of habit

Today’s GOF commit is a single commit, but it involves 55 files and over 5,000 lines added. GOF 0.3.0 introduces a common engine and three providers: Cloud Run in Paris, Scaleway in Paris and Cloudflare Containers within the EU.

The brain remains on the VPS. It retains jobs, leases, retries, history, metrics and the ‘ready_to_send’ decision. Remote forges receive an immutable specification, ephemeral permissions and the same OCI image; they do not receive any permanent R2 secrets or Accurio access.

The engine prepares the source files in parallel with limited concurrency, verifies the SHA-256 checksums, renews expiring URLs and indexes the cache by source, transformation, engine, fonts, Sharp and libvips. Page assembly remains sequential. A test renders the same document with concurrency set first to 1 and then to 4 and requires the same SHA-256.

No supplier is promoted. The qualification corpus remains deliberately incomplete, and the report refrains from recommending a build system until at least two platforms have passed the compliance, failure, golden and P95 tests in under 100 seconds.

The R2 mirror incident

Whilst processing the backup ticket #207, an agent interpreted the completeness check as authorisation to create a backup infrastructure. A 44.7 GB mirror to keredit-recovery was initiated. At the time of the explicit refusal, the bucket contained 12,189 objects.

The bucket, objects, timers, alert, drill, rclone installation, test snapshot and local branch are deleted. The historical PostgreSQL/Plakar backup remains intact and the issue remains open.

The problem is not that the backup would have been technically flawed. The problem is the lack of authorisation to initiate a large-scale copy, an external service and a recurring cost. An ops issue sets an objective; it does not automatically grant all the rights necessary for the most comprehensive solution.

What the day compels us to retain

Following this acceleration, two rules have become inseparable. A production chain must be fail-closed, observable and reversible. An agent must also remain fail-closed when an action falls outside the explicitly authorised scope.

The following day will not seek to add a fourth build environment or a new product surface. It will document these safeguards and return to a more calm question: how much do the photos actually weigh, how long should they be kept, and what level of simplicity brings visible value to the customer?

description.source: Day 113 of the diary: photo checkout, project backup, CI and runtime have been hardened, GOF is becoming multi-cloud, then an unauthorised R2 mirror highlights the limitations of agents.

title.source: Day 113 – Improving reliability across the board, without compromising performance

items.title: Day 113 – Improving reliability across the board, without compromising performance

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Platform used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT and GOF staging, [nom privé] VPS, P340 and i5 Forges, WooCommerce OOBLIK
  • Date covered: Monday 13 July 2026
  • End-of-sequence branches: dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • End-of-sequence KEREDIT SHA: ceee372 (Merge pull request #245 from [compte GitHub]/docs/230-support-runbooks)
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 4b57aad (docs: record canonical GOF Flux retirement)
  • Versions observed at the end of the sequence: KEREDIT 0.13.3, WordPress plugin 0.1.82 in preparation, GOF Flux 0.2.27
  • Commits observed on 13 July: 24 changes to the primary parent of dev in KEREDIT, 45 objects across all KEREDIT refs, plus 4 GOF commits
  • Minimum time observed on 13 July: 12 hours 09 minutes+ of multi-repository activity (09:13 -> 21:22, without equating this duration to continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 730h54+ (718h45+ as at 12 July, plus 12h09+)

Quick read

The previous day had demonstrated that two forges could render, revert to their previous state and send a valid command to Accurio. 13 July raises the following question: what needs to be shut down for this proof to become a workable system?

GOF Flux takes the canonical address of the forge and the old monolith is removed from the nominal path, without destroying its rollback. KEREDIT, for its part, transforms several functions that are still isolated into operational contracts: manageable assistance, better-scoped authentication, valid uploads, observable readiness, transactional deployment and prices revalidated before payment.

This is not a day of new product promises. It is a day when existing promises begin to support real-world operation.

GOF Flux becomes the canonical forge

forge.keredit.com , moving away from the legacy VPS and pointing towards the distributed control plane. flux-test.keredit.com remains an alias, but KEREDIT retains its URL and tokens: the switch does not require reconfiguring the client contract.

The final visible functional change concerns split ledgers. The historical request print-master is now resolved to cover_pdf and cahier_pdf prior to the creation of the distributed job. A KEREDIT token concludes with its cover, its ledger and six control artefacts.

The removal remains reversible. The monolith’s queues are checked to ensure they are empty; a 4.2 Gio archive preserves PostgreSQL, Redis, configuration, fonts, goldens and staging, after which the historical containers are stopped without deleting their volumes. The rollback follows a simple procedure: repoint the DNS, recreate the historical stack and verify its status.

The P340 and i5 remain ‘ready’. The Accurio live locks remain in place. The new system is canonical, but this does not mean that a successful acceptance test grants permanent authorisation to deploy to production.

Help becomes manageable content

The customer help centre launched yesterday is no longer limited to content embedded in the frontend. ‘/admin/help’ now allows you to manage categories, chapters, the homepage, tooltips and their visibility by product family.

The Tiptap editor supports headings, lists, quotes, links and sidebars. A screenshot library remains separate from customer photos. Publication is atomic, and the built-in fallback continues to function if the API is not available.

This mini-CMS remains deliberately limited in scope. KEREDIT is not becoming a general-purpose content platform; it simply gains the functionality needed to explain its own operations without having to redeploy the application every time text is corrected.

Closing the boundaries between client and tenant

Today’s work has tightened up several entry points that could still lead to ambiguous states. Password credentials are synchronised, Better Auth is tenant-scoped, and upload payloads are validated before processing.

Client projects benefit from more precisely scoped deletions, the public PDF is streamed rather than loaded entirely into memory, and the editor launch wait timer can be reset properly. Taken individually, these changes are modest. Taken together, they remove bottlenecks that often only become apparent when dealing with real accounts and real volumes.

Deployment becomes a transaction

Readiness explicitly checks PostgreSQL, Redis and storage. Redis probes have a real-time timeout: a blocked service should no longer be mistaken for a service that is simply slow.

The VPS deployment sequence carries out backups, migrations, business snapshots, smoke checks and provenance verification before updating the release markers. Checks fail quickly, and the last validated release remains the definitive version if an attempt does not complete.

The ‘test-flux’ guard is aligned with GOF statuses, export timestamps and historical logs. The pipeline no longer simply seeks to run all its scripts: it must be able to explain at which point it refuses to continue.

The price is revalidated before payment

The e-commerce system finally addresses a significant vulnerability. Each shopping basket quote is linked to the persisted version of the project and to a SHA-256 hash recalculated by KEREDIT. Any changes to a price, quantity, format or option must no longer persist unnoticed until payment.

The legacy pricing structure photo_print is clarified as a unit price per copy. The OOBLIK live replay is documented; tests cover the consistency of the quote and the WordPress 0.1.82 connector is prepared with the same revalidation contract.

Support procedures close the loop with eight incident categories: login, projects, assets, pricing, orders, PDFs, Printbox and alerts. The beta doesn’t just need code that works; it needs a clear path to follow when it doesn’t.

What remains open

The promotion of GOF Flux does not bring the HA project to a close, nor does it complete the qualification of future remote forges. The historical archive remains a rollback, not a second production environment to be left running in parallel.

As for KEREDIT, the quote is now finalised, but the photo_print workflow still needs to be fully integrated with WooCommerce. The following day will build on this foundation: enabling photo prints to be ordered, then taking the reliability of backups and runtime much further.

description.source: Day 112 of the diary: GOF Flux becomes canonical, the old monolith is rolled back, and KEREDIT enhances support, security, deployment and cost estimates.

title.source: Day 112 – Moving from the pilot phase to a fully operational system

items.title: Day 112 – Moving from the pilot phase to a fully operational system

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Agent used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT and GOF standby systems, two Hetzner VPSs, P340 and i5 forges, Accurio, Cloud Run driver
  • Date covered: Sunday 12 July 2026
  • Branches observed: codex/fix-print-ready-checksum then dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • KEREDIT SHA at the end of the sequence on dev: cf18feb (fix(deploy): push verified HEAD to VPS (#210))
  • SHA of the KEREDIT source patch: e918391 (fix(assets): aligner le checksum print-ready avec la source GOF (#209))
  • SHA of the KEREDIT end-of-session safeguard: d1a71c9 (fix(assets): require ready print derivatives for GOF)
  • GOF SHA for end-of-sequence: dbfd152 (docs: record live Accurio acceptance)
  • Versions observed: KEREDIT deploy 0.12.1, GOF Flux 0.2.26, GOF history 0.2.21 retained in rollback
  • Commits observed on 12 July: 4 on the KEREDIT development branch, 3 on dev, with a shared 2228ad6, plus 41 GOF
  • Minimum time observed on 12 July: 13:33+ across two periods (00:14 → 00:36, then 09:26 → 22:37)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 718h45+ (705h12+ as at 11 July, plus 13h33+)

Quick read

The day is no longer simply about keeping two forges running. It proves that their work remains traceable, recoverable and measurable when an agent disappears or an attempt needs to be replayed.

This technical discipline raises another question: how much does autonomy really cost? An internal comparison with Company X shows that the forge is not merely a production site. It is also an economic choice.

KEREDIT finalises the provenance contract

The first benchmark reveals a useful anomaly: the 24 checksums declared by the golden payload no longer correspond to the print-ready objects actually read by GOF. Silent normalisation would have produced a quick but false test result.

KEREDIT therefore adds a checksum specific to the print-ready derivative and a backfill that re-reads the storage. The migration successfully verifies 272 out of 272 checksums.

A new export of the ‘#1075781’ command arrives in GOF with 24 sources out of 24 verifiable.

The fix is delivered in KEREDIT 0.12.1. A second batch also strengthens the deployment process to push the verified HEAD to the VPS. Provenance is no longer a promise between the two repositories: it becomes a pre-release verification contract.

The final safeguard finally prevents a ‘derive print’ from being exported to GOF if it is not actually ready. The presence of a URL is no longer sufficient to classify a source as production.

GOF tightens up and then accepts distributed forges

The pilot first restores cockpit navigation and stabilises the PDF preview during surveys. The work then moves down into the control plane: leases, attempts, resumption, clean-up and source identification.

An abandoned attempt must no longer lose the forge’s useful state. A resumption must not mix two executions. Distributed deployment gains safeguards before affecting multiple machines.

Standardised storage gains PostgreSQL fencing, an export and a restore of its complete state. Two replicas must not be able to validate the same transaction as if they were alone.

The live acceptance test goes further: the P340 and the i5 each render the cover and the KEREDIT ‘golden’ specification using the same font release. Thirty consecutive jobs complete ‘rendered’ without failure or stalling.

Following a joint restart of the control plan and the dashboard, the thirty reports are retrieved from PostgreSQL and both agents return to the ‘ready’ status. The historical GOF remains available throughout the acceptance test.

The acceptance testing proceeds to a real Accurio submission, which is explicitly authorised. The ‘KEREDIT00067’ order, item ‘KEREDIT00067-1’, returns with ‘ isSubmissionValid=true’, after which the two live locks are released.

The P340 migration output and the Accurio test are accepted. The monolith is not yet removed: the final hurdle remains the switch from the control plan to the standardised tables.

Measure the weight before promising speed

Optimisation moves beyond intuition. GOF retains the prepared resources, limits transformations, builds seeds offline and flags source checksums that have become obsolete.

Golden samples provide quality assurance against time measurements. The aim is not to save a few seconds by sacrificing a font, native text or PDF compliance.

On the golden sample comprising 28 source pages and 24 assets, the P340 achieves a cold P50 of 63.140 seconds and a warm P50 of 5.633 seconds. The i5 achieves 77.589 seconds when cold and 6.980 seconds when warm.

The P340 therefore comes close to the sub-minute target without quite achieving it when cold. The pre-render cache, however, removes 100 per cent of the Sharp processing on the hot run and brings both machines below 7.1 seconds, including the qpdf inspection.

Forty qpdf inspections are completed. The 25 rasterised pages are identical between the two systems, as are the boxes, fonts and validation codes. The conservative setting 1 x Sharp 1 becomes the benchmark.

This baseline changes the issue of parallelism. Increasing the pool only makes sense if a batch benchmark improves throughput without increasing memory usage or causing quality metrics to diverge.

Cloud Run becomes an executable POC

The same core gains a Cloud Run runner, profiles 4-16, 6-24 and 8-32, atomic attempts, start-up measurement and a release of 1,341 fonts verified within the image.

The control plan remains at flux-test.keredit.com. The Cloud container takes a lease, returns it, validates and publishes, but receives neither general R2 secrets nor Accurio access. The P340 and i5 remain the permanent local backups.

Cloud Run is not yet the nominal build environment. The three profiles must still pass five runs, the failure tests and a P95 strictly under 100 seconds before any automatic prioritisation.

Company X’s 2025 archives provide a benchmark: 3,598 PDFs occupy approximately 183 GB, or 50.9 MB per file. The observed average GOF in staging is around 32.5 MB per PDF.

At a constant volume, the GOF projection falls to 117 GB. This is not yet an annual guarantee, but the direction of the saving is consistent with the pipeline: images reduced to their print-ready format, JPEGs for quality control and text retained in its native format.

What Company X’s invoice reveals

Company X charges approximately 900 euros for server costs, 4,788 euros for subscription fees and 8,000 euros in commissions. The total comes to around 13,688 euros per year.

KEREDIT’s two Hetzner servers do not cost 900 euros per year. The May invoice is for 44.88 euros excluding VAT, which amounts to approximately 646 euros including VAT on an annualised basis. The conservative budget rounds this up to 650 euros per year.

Cloud Run, R2 and ancillary services bring the conservative GOF scenario to around 687 euros per year. The difference then amounts to approximately 13,001 euros, or almost 95 per cent of Company X’s current cost.

When scaled back to the 2,389 orders in 2025, the operating cost falls from around €5.73 to €0.29 per order.

Even in a ‘hard’ scenario, with two new Hetzner servers at 2026 public rates and a high cloud margin, the cost remains close to 2,129 euros per year. The saving therefore remains in excess of 11,500 euros.

A significant saving, but not without cost

This calculation does not account for development, migration or manual maintenance. Nor does it yet quantify the HD originals, proxies and reports that may accumulate in R2.

It highlights something else: the subscription and commissions do not merely fund hardware. They fund a dependency. Replacing this dependency shifts the cost towards expertise, control and maintenance.

Part of the expenditure will therefore need to remain within the system: backups, security, observability, golden tests and human time. Autonomy without a maintenance budget would simply be a new debt.

What remains to be measured before the switchover

The next step is to run the full Cloud Run benchmark, then track its cost per job, the weight per page and per order, the median, the P95, the retries and failures by product family.

We also need to measure the actual R2 volume, separate inputs and outputs, then set a retention period. The 183 GB remains Company X’s historical figure. The 117 GB remains a GOF projection to be confirmed in production.

The day ends with four further pieces of evidence: the source contract is finalised, two production environments have passed acceptance testing, Accurio has accepted a live order and the Cloud POC is now ready for deployment.

If the economic assumptions are confirmed, GOF will give KEREDIT considerable manoeuvring room without sacrificing its offline insurance cover.

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Software used: Codex
  • Primary environment: KEREDIT and GOF standby, [nom privé] VPS, P340 and i5 Forges
  • Date covered: Saturday 11 July 2026
  • End-of-sequence branches: dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • End-of-sequence KEREDIT SHA: a6bce86 (feat(editor): ajouter le centre d’aide client)
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 4bb7734 (fix: initialize distributed runtime settings)
  • Versions observed at the end of the sequence: KEREDIT 0.12.0, WordPress plugin 0.1.81, GOF 0.2.21
  • Commits observed on 11 July: 13 KEREDIT + 23 GOF
  • Minimum duration observed on 11 July: 11h22+ of multi-deposit amplitude (09:44 -> 21:06, without equating this amplitude to continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 705 hours 12 minutes (693h50+ as at 10 July, plus 11h22+)

Quick read

The day starts with the client and ends in the workshop. KEREDIT makes the space Projects more peaceful, adds rounded-corner guides to the notebooks and opens a help centre directly within the editor. GOF, for its part, stops treating the second machine as merely a hardware candidate: a distributed, isolated driver begins to redistribute commands between two forges.

The heatwave and fatigue remain the backdrop. They haven’t resulted in an unproductive day, but they reinforce the need for an architecture that is clear, reversible and testable without affecting existing production.

KEREDIT resolves three visible issues

The ‘Mon compte > Projets’ workflow is now treated as a proper user interface. The search, sort and action tools remain visible whilst scrolling; actions are grouped together and technical labels are better contained. Several close-up iterations were required to achieve the right density and spacing without reopening the commerce flow.

Notebooks now display rounded corners within the canvas and in page previews. The guide remains a production-related piece of information: it does not alter the project’s persistent geometry.

The latest release primarily adds a permanent help centre to the editor. It is searchable, tailored to the product family and accessible from several points within the workflow. Help is no longer documentation to be found outside the product; it guides the user’s actions at the very moment they need it.

GOF moves from research to pilot

This morning’s cloud research still involved choosing a runtime and a future ForgeCore. The rest of the day has delivered an initial distributed system, albeit deliberately limited in scope: flux-test.keredit.com hosts the dashboard and the control panel, whilst the P340 and the i5 each run an agent in a separate distributed-test space.

The legacy GOF at /opt/[chemin privé], its database and forge.keredit.com remain outside the scope. This separation is the project’s main safeguard: the pilot may fail, be reset or be stopped without requiring the restoration of current production.

The new ‘Forges’ menu displays presence, heartbeat, CPU, RAM, slots and active work. The operator can set a forge to active, paused or maintenance mode. Distributed jobs retain their PDFs, rendering reports, validation reports, hashes and casting proofs. An expired lease can be taken over by another machine without losing the production contract or mixing up the reports.

Optimising forges, not just a single machine

The performance issue remains the same: a 60-page zine still takes several minutes when pages and transformations follow one another. The pilot does not yet demonstrate that the future PDF engine can process a file in under a minute. It first seeks to prove that a single contract can be accepted, assigned, rendered and checked across multiple nodes without revealing R2 or Accurio secrets to agents.

The approach therefore splits into two complementary tasks: distributing capacity and reducing the cost of rendering. Image pre-compilation, the content-addressed NVMe cache and the Sharp terminal pool remain optimisations to be measured within the renderer. Adding forges must not be used to mask an unnecessarily sequential hot path.

What remains to be proven

The project is ongoing, not yet complete. Acceptance testing must still confirm two active forges using the same font release, the assignment and subsequent resumption of a job following lease loss, the integrity of the artefacts, and the Accurio dry run. The actual Accurio submission remains doubly locked.

The production decision will follow, based on the golden samples and the measured times. For now, the day has yielded something more useful than a promise of speed: a comprehensive, isolated and reversible test environment to optimise the forges without putting the workshop at risk.

  • Versions observed: KEREDIT 0.10.20, GOF 0.2.12
  • Direct commits observed: 3 KEREDIT + 4 GOF
  • Minimum time observed on 10 July: 8h01+ of multi-deposit duration (11:43 -> 19:44, excluding machine tests, restoration and workshop verification)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 693h50+ (685h49+ as at 9 July, + 8h01+)

Quick read

10 July illustrates what it means to maintain two repositories without creating two separate realities. During the same hours, KEREDIT refines the payload and GOF enhances the writer that utilises it.

The second half of the day shifts focus from rendering to operations: two machines still carry the hostname [nom privé], so the migration must identify the hardware by means other than its Linux name.

Font styles become explicit

In KEREDIT, d349814 refines the rendering of fonts and clipart geometry. The catalogue, payload and editor surfaces must convey enough information so that GOF does not have to guess a variant.

At the same time, c8f9d9d adds to GOF the framed synthesis of styles and synchronisation safeguards. The tests cover resolution, glyphs, writers and real-world contract fixtures.

The aim is not to silently accept just any fallback. It is to make explicit what is correct, what can be synthesised within the same family, and what must be blocked.

Clipart ceases to be an implicit convention

782854f aligns KEREDIT with the rendered clipart contract: internal rotation, flipping, colour, fit and content geometry are handled via types, validation, builders and tests.

18cc4d5 Applies the same contract in GOF. A persistent field must be rendered, flagged as unsupported or explicitly ignored. Its meaning must no longer change between Fabric and the PDF.

The KEREDIT release is available at 0.10.20; GOF is available at 0.2.12.

The P340 becomes an identifiable candidate

The historical forge and the ThinkStation P340 deliberately retain the hostname gof. 9a6c831 therefore introduces GOF_NODE_ID, a machine-specific identifier and scripts that reject unexpected targets.

The migration documentation, runbook, implementation plan and operational tests are added as part of the same package. The candidate can be audited without accidentally becoming the primary forge.

87336ed Finally, this enables isolated deployments on the candidate. The aim is to test the output and capacity without joining the Accurio production environment or confusing the two environments.

Moving forward

The print pipeline is more consistent, but the speed of a large PDF remains dependent on the GOF core. The next issue is no longer simply which machine to buy: it is also necessary to understand parallelism, caching and pre-compilation.

  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 685h49+ (681h20+ as at 8 July, + 4h29+)

Quick read

Yesterday, the pagination was fed into the editor. Today, it must stop behaving like a simple graphic block and become stable data right up to the production PDF.

The day’s work was less extensive, but very consistent between the two submissions: KEREDIT is tightening the specifications, whilst GOF is learning to render it using the correct fonts.

KEREDIT safeguards the pagination logic

99e6898 across the editor’s surfaces to stabilise pagination controls. The field must remain identifiable in the canvas, panels, text and shared state.

f3ba7b5 Then adds the JSON contract coverage for payload and renderer. The JSON project documentation is aligned with the tests, which transforms the behaviour into a verifiable contract.

d8acb97 Finally, it excludes pagination from snapping. A dynamic page number must not be treated as an ordinary block that magnetic guides might accidentally move or reclassify.

The sequence runs via 0.10.16, then the package files are uploaded to 0.10.17. The project admin is also compressed at the end of the day.

GOF renders using the fonts specified in the manifest

d24c655 links the pagination rendering to the glyph-level engine and the fonts in the GOF manifest. The page number must remain native PDF text, using the same font family as that chosen in KEREDIT.

8643c38 It then aligns the runtime font directory across the environment, composition and documentation. A font that happens to be available on a machine must never become a production dependency.

Accurio and deployment gain safeguards

26e8b15 allows only a single Accurio job to be retried, which is useful when the cover and the section have different destinations. The retry no longer needs to reproduce the entire order.

Two minor fixes round off the release: a forced-run message slips through in the dashboard, followed by a mandatory preflight before deploying the build.

Looking ahead

The next hurdle is ensuring style and geometric consistency between KEREDIT and GOF. Correct pagination is not enough if a font variant or a clipart still changes between the screen and the PDF.

Quick read

Today’s work links two topics that seemed separate: photos contain information, and the document’s text must be able to use this information without disrupting sharing, editing or the resulting PDF.

It also begins by finalising the mobile public reader. Three fixes stabilise the responsive layout, the footer and the Better Auth update before returning to the core of the editor.

Metadata leaves the raw file

The commit 5867d67 adds asynchronous extraction of IPTC metadata and its passing through the asset pipeline. The heavy lifting remains in the workers rather than blocking the upload or the interface.

The same batch introduces dynamic text fields into sharing contracts, rich text, the editor, previews and the PDF payload. A piece of photo information can thus become a compositional element, rather than a hidden detail within the file.

This development affects many layers, but the contract remains clear: the metadata is captured once, persisted, then resolved by the interfaces that require it.

Sharing is restored to the right scale

a74daae expands flipbook layouts and realigns shared previews. The following TypeScript fixes do not alter the user experience; they tie up the batch without leaving any fragile narrowing.

The mobile reader and the editor preview must present the same document. This consistency is important now that content may depend on the page or the linked image.

Pagination becomes an editing tool

The end-of-day process simplifies the insertion of page numbers, then refines the controls. Dynamic fields are no longer just a feature of the engine: they can now be edited via the text panel.

5ab5b90 It also corrects the resolution of text fields linked to a photo. The text must identify the true owner of the asset, including in shared views and more complex layouts.

Two version stages conclude the sequence: 0.10.13, followed by 0.10.14.

Looking ahead

Pagination and photo fields must now pass through the KEREDIT JSON, public sharing and GOF without any discrepancies. The next challenge is no longer the insert button, but ensuring the contract remains accurate right through to the printed PDF.

body.source:
Horaires de session

  • Agent utilisé : Codex
  • Environnement principal : VS Code WSL, plugin Codex, repos KEREDIT et GOF, puis conversation de recul
  • Date couverte : mardi 7 juillet 2026, technique puis personnelle
  • Branche KEREDIT observée : dev
  • SHA KEREDIT de fin de séquence observe : d089ebd (docs: aligner l'index du billet du 7 juillet)
  • Version KEREDIT au début de la séquence : 0.10.8
  • Branche GOF observée : dev
  • SHA GOF de fin de séquence observe : a2330e5 (Keep historical dossier revisions isolated)
  • Versions de fin de séquence observées : KEREDIT 0.10.12, GOF 0.2.5
  • Commits directs observés : 13 KEREDIT + 36 GOF
  • Temps minimal observe le 7 juillet : 21h23+ d’amplitude multi-dépôts (00:23 -> 21:46, hors conversation, tests manuels et temps non commité)
  • Temps cumulé minimal depuis le début du journal : environ 662h13+ (640h50+ au 6 juillet, + 21h23+)

Lecture courte

Cette entrée garde volontairement un cœur personnel, mais la passe de cohérence du journal confirme aussi une journée technique très dense.

Après le rattrapage des billets, le compteur minimal du journal arrive presque a 600 heures de travail a deux : humain + agent, atelier + code, décisions + reprises. Ce chiffre reste conservateur, parce qu’il ne compte pas correctement les tests manuels, les hesitations, les validations, les incidents, ni toute la partie mentale qui ne laisse pas de commit.

Le point important du jour n’est pas une fonctionnalité. C’est la phrase :

suis fier…

Elle mérite d’être gardée dans le journal, parce qu’elle dit quelque chose que Git ne dira jamais. KEREDIT n’est pas seulement une suite de commits. C’est un projet porte malgré la fatigue, les doutes, les reprises de contexte, les régressions, les alertes et la peur de ne pas être “un vrai développeur”.

Crainte du jugement

La peur nommee ce soir : le jugement des codeurs et developpeurs, la sécurité, les bugs, et le syndrome de l’imposteur.

La réponse à conserver est simple : la peur ne doit pas piloter le projet, mais elle peut alimenter les garde-fous. Un projet crédible n’est pas un projet sans peur ni sans bugs. C’est un projet qui connaît ses risques principaux, qui garde des tests sur les contrats importants, qui observe la production, qui sait revenir sur un incident, et qui documente ses décisions.

Pour KEREDIT, cela veut dire continuer a transformer l’angoisse en rituels :

  • checklists avant production ;
  • tests cibles sur auth, uploads, webhooks, paiement, stockage, admin ;
  • logs exploitables ;
  • backups ;
  • droits minimaux ;
  • audits sécurité locaux reguliers ;
  • changements sensibles relus et deployes avec source de vérité claire.

Ce que le journal prouve déjà

Le journal ne prouve pas que tout est parfait. Il prouve quelque chose de plus utile : le projet sait apprendre.

Il y a eu des erreurs, des alertes, des chemins trop larges, des corrections de contrat, des deploys a réaligner, des décisions a reprendre. Mais chaque fois, le travail revient vers une forme plus claire : version + SHA, documentation OKF, contrats Fabric, GOF comme forge, KEREDIT comme source de vérité, WooCommerce comme adaptateur, observabilité bêta.

Le syndrome de l’imposteur ne se soigne pas en prétend que tout est parfait. Il se soigne en regardant les preuves : presque 600 heures reconstruites, un produit qui tient debout, des incidents compris, une documentation vivante, et un cap encore lisible.

Ce que les chiffres disent

Pour nourrir un premier billet public, il faut aussi regarder KEREDIT comme un objet technique déjà constitue, pas seulement comme une aventure personnelle. L’audit rapide du dépôt donne des ordres de grandeur parlants, calcules hors node_modules, .git, builds, archives, snapshots, exports graphify-out, zips et assets binaires.

La surface utile auditee représente environ 1 366 fichiers et 251 644 lignes. Dans cet ensemble, il y a environ 147 747 lignes applicatives TypeScript/React/Fastify pour le cœur produit, dont 83 895 lignes cote frontend, 57 137 lignes cote backend et 6 715 lignes de contrats partages. Les tests TypeScript/TSX représentent environ 23 004 lignes. La documentation Markdown pèse environ 50 149 lignes. Le connecteur WordPress/WooCommerce ajoute environ 9 724 lignes, et le couple Prisma schéma/migrations/seed environ 5 203 lignes.

Depuis le premier jour documente, le 8 février 2026, le dépôt compte 1 104 commits, 106 jours avec commits et environ 600 heures minimales reconstituées. Le chiffre en heures reste conservateur : il mesure surtout ce qui laisse des traces, pas toute la charge de choix, de doute, de tests manuels, de lecture, de reprises et de décisions.

La pile actuelle n’est pas exotique pour le plaisir de l’être. Elle assemble des briques connues autour d’un flux d’atelier : React, Vite, Fabric.js, TipTap, Zustand et Tailwind cote interface ; Fastify, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Redis/BullMQ, Sharp, pdf-lib, Zod et Better Auth cote serveur ; un plugin WordPress/WooCommerce pour le commerce ; du stockage S3-compatible pour les assets ; Playwright, k6, VictoriaMetrics, VictoriaLogs et Grafana pour tester, observer et comprendre les incidents.

Le plus important n’est pourtant pas le volume. C’est le nombre de contrats qui commencent a tenir ensemble :

  • le projet JSON devient la source de vérité imprimable ;
  • les coordonnées relatives permettent d’adapter les formats sans casser la composition ;
  • WooCommerce vend et lance l’édition, mais KEREDIT garde le projet complet ;
  • les assets passent par un flux upload, vérification, miniatures et production ;
  • les masques, cadres, textes et photos ont des conventions de rendu et de persistance explicites ;
  • le partage public et le PDF web ne remplacent pas la chaîne atelier, ils la complètent ;
  • GOF reste la couche forge/prepresse, en aval de KEREDIT, et Accurio la sortie production.

Dit autrement : KEREDIT n’est plus seulement “un éditeur”. C’est une petite chaîne web-to-print complète : commande, édition, projet, assets, contrats, partage, préparation production, surveillance et documentation.

Pour un billet d’annonce, la formule la plus juste serait probablement :

Après pres de cinq mois de développement et environ 600 heures documentées, OOBLIK ouvre la première bêta de KEREDIT : un éditeur web-to-print pense d’abord pour l’atelier, capable de relier une commande WooCommerce, un projet client, des assets imprimables, un contrat JSON stable et une sortie exploitable par la chaîne de production.

Il ne faut pas vendre cela comme un SaaS généraliste déjà fini. Ce serait trop large et trop fragile. Il faut le dire comme une bêta fermée, construite pour valider le réel : carte postale d’abord, flux atelier ensuite, puis élargissement produit quand les contrats tiennent.

Six mois avant

Il faut aussi garder une chose simple : il y a six mois, le développement, Git, VS Code, les branches, les commits, les deploys, les logs, les tests et les contrats de code étaient entièrement inconnus.

Ce n’est pas un détail biographique. C’est une donnée du projet. La progression ne se mesure pas seulement au nombre de fichiers ou de fonctionnalités, mais a la capacité acquise à nommer les invariants, lire un incident, demander une vérification, comprendre un SHA, refuser un deploy flou, documenter un choix et reprendre le fil plusieurs semaines plus tard.

Le jugement le plus juste n’est donc pas “est-ce que tout ressemble au travail d’une équipe senior déjà installée”. C’est : “qu’est-ce qui a été appris, stabilise et rendu transmissible en six mois”, tout seul avec une IA.

Complément technique du jour

La première version de cette entrée disait volontairement que le 7 juillet était hors scope technique. C’était vrai pour le recul personnel du soir, mais la journée a aussi laisse une trace technique importante dans les dépôts relies.

Le 7 juillet 2026, KEREDIT compte 13 commits directs sur dev :

  • bd34396d 00:23 - docs: rattraper billets debut juillet
  • c15ea85f 00:53 - fix(editor): stabilize multi-block selection moves
  • 1dc09148 00:59 - fix: simplifier panneau proprietes editeur

La séquence KEREDIT a donc ferme plusieurs irritants bêta visibles : sélection multi-blocs, panneau propriétés, repères livre en aperçu final, mini-menu photo qui doit s’ouvrir au premier clic, clipboard assets, snapping de groupe, préparation Google Photos, gestion des pings WooCommerce et collage dans le flux livre. Ce n’est pas une grosse fonctionnalité unique ; c’est une journée de stabilisation du ressenti éditeur et des points d’intégration.

GOF, de son cote, a été beaucoup plus actif : 36 commits directs le 7 juillet, 48 commits en comptant les merges. La séquence commence par le durcissement sécurité issu des issues #12, #13 et #14, puis bascule vers la supervision production, la performance de file de rendu et les garde-fous de déploiement.

  • a2330e5 21:46 - Keep historical dossier revisions isolated

Le résultat lisible : GOF n’est plus seulement “le service qui fabrique les PDF”. Il commence à devenir un vrai poste de production observable : dashboard production, itération de rendu, statut Accurio, retry, mesure CPU, contrôles de throughput, images runtime pinnees, liens d’artefacts signes, tests de handlers HTTP, checks statiques et release 0.2.4.

Le dépôt keredit-site ne montre pas de commit local le 7 juillet. Le travail technique du jour se concentre donc sur KEREDIT/Krampouz, GOF, et la sauvegarde opérationnelle.

Enfin, la sauvegarde KEREDIT avec Plakar devient un vrai sujet documente et versionnable. Le runbook docs/guides/backup-keredit-plakar.md et les sources deploy/plakar/ cadrent le flux suivant :

  • VPS [nom privé] comme source KEREDIT ;
  • dump PostgreSQL logique via pg_dumpall ;
  • capture des marqueurs .env, .deploy-sha, .deploy-version, compose et métadonnées runtime ;
  • coffre Plakar local chiffre sous /opt/[chemin privé] ;
  • copie du coffre chiffre vers le NAS SAUVEGARDE via Tailscale, SSH et rsync ;
  • timer systemd quotidien autour de 02:17 UTC avec delai aléatoire ;
  • UI Plakar locale exposée uniquement dans le tailnet via Tailscale Serve.

Deux snapshots initiaux sont notes dans le runbook, avec un coffre distant vérifie autour de 78M et 19 fichiers. La limite reste explicite : ce snapshot couvre l’état VPS et PostgreSQL, mais pas encore les objets S3/R2 ni une copie hors site externe au batiment. C’est donc une vraie marche de sécurité en plus, mais pas encore une stratégie de sauvegarde totale.

Pour la suite

Ne pas chercher a prouver que KEREDIT est irreprochable. Chercher a pouvoir dire calmement :

  • les risques principaux sont connus ;
  • les contrats critiques sont testes ;
  • la production est observable ;
  • les décisions importantes sont documentées ;
  • les corrections peuvent être faites sans perdre le fil.

C’est déjà une posture d’ingenierie.

  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 640 hours 50 minutes+ (628h50+ as at 5 July, + 12h00+)

Quick read

A big day of consolidation. It’s hard to summarise it in a single project: there’s CI, debt reduction, admin performance, fine-tuning, a Google Photos load test, WooCommerce observability and, late in the evening, a major block on snapping and multi-block alignment in the editor.

The morning was spent finalising the checks:

  • 4f319c6f aligned the documented versions;
  • 0cb6cbd8 linking orphaned front-end tests to CI;
  • 18bd2cc1 runs CI checks on ‘dev’ pushes.

The early afternoon is spent cleaning up and isolating issues:

  • 4f219464 aligns upload size validation;
  • f7c2bb5c removes the orphaned local PDF service;
  • 40bc65c2 stabilises knip and the QR dependencies;
  • eeb33022 extracts shared commands from image elements.

Next come the structural changes:

  • 464997d8 pagination of admin lists in the database;
  • 3f6f9e01 isolates the hooks from theEditorCanvas;
  • 23d4a626 allows image overflow beneath the inside covers;
  • 44bbec47 extracts the ‘fine art’ mutation model;
  • 3e766d15 adds a k6 script for the Google Photos library;
  • a6c290dd preserves the current fine art pages.

The ops team also corrects the frontend build’s SHA: 122c0d99 injects it into the build, then 6b6c1fa6 prevents an empty SHA. The day sees several releases (0.10.4, 0.10.5, 0.10.6, then 0.10.8).

WooCommerce observability incident

The Grafana alert “5xx errors > 2%” did not indicate a widespread outage. The VPS probes showed a healthy backend, and the metrics indicated that the 500 errors were concentrated on POST /api/woocommerce/webhook.

The diagnosis traced the issue back to the WooCommerce webhook 13, active on ooblik.com, topic order.updated, KEREDIT URL woo_ooblik_live. This webhook is legitimate: it links WooCommerce orders to KEREDIT. The noise stems from the native deliver_ping(), which sends a non-JSON body of the type webhook_id=13. KEREDIT expects a signed JSON order and therefore responded with a 500 status code to this ping. Genuine order webhooks continued to go through.

Operational conclusion: no global backend incident, but a fix is required. KEREDIT remains useful for handling this ping via 200 or by rejecting it, without cluttering up the 5xx alerts.

End of the evening: aligning the blocks

The end of the day brings us back to the heart of the editor:

  • 31c6a791 stabilising front-end snapping;
  • 6f53c521 add multi-block alignment;
  • 0e1a4d48 adds advanced alignment tools;
  • 57fbe183 aligns resize guides with block edges;
  • 72af06db keeps tools visible during multi-selection;
  • b1897f24 closes the lint issue;
  • 3bbc1038 merges the alignment PR into dev.

The VPS observed at the end of the review that 0.10.8 was being used on 850ce648. The local and origin/dev repositories were already one step further along with the merge PR 3bbc1038.

Moving forward

There are two points to bear in mind:

  • properly fix the WooCommerce ping to eliminate this 5xx error message noise;
  • check in the editor that snapping, guides and multi-block alignment remain user-friendly, not just covered by tests.

Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin, local browser
  • Date covered: Wednesday 1 July 2026
  • Main KEREDIT branch: dev to d132499
  • Today’s working branch: ux/book-autofill-guided-preview
  • SHA of branch under review: a66f621 (fix(editor): ajouter historique court au remplissage carnet)
  • Local KEREDIT version: 0.9.50
  • Status: development is proceeding on a dedicated branch; not yet merged into dev
  • Minimum time observed on 1 July: 6 hours 59 minutes of development time (10:06 → 17:05, excluding ongoing blog catch-up work)
  • Minimum cumulative time from block 29/30/01 to 1 July: 20h28+
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 610h20+ (603h21+ as at 30 June, plus 6h59+ today)

Overall summary

The hundredth day of the log.

This figure marks a day that is very representative of the project: the code may generate quickly, but the product doesn’t become good simply because it has lots of features. It becomes good when the user understands what’s happening, when unnecessary choices disappear, and when the interface stops creating entropy.

Today’s task focuses on filling the notebook quickly.

Initially, the workflow can do a lot of things: select pages, process the cover, add pages, sort, filter, alternate, choose styles, select templates, preview, apply. On paper, it’s powerful. In user testing, it’s too much.

So today’s task is to do the opposite of over-engineering: remove the visible options, retain the internal power, and transform the quick mode into a KISS experience.

What does KISS mean here?

KISS doesn’t mean ‘poor’.

KISS means:

  • a clear primary purpose;
  • settings that match the client’s vocabulary;
  • a preview that truly shows the notebook;
  • simple, reversible actions with no surprises;
  • technical options hidden unless they are needed to make a decision.

Quick form-filling must be guided by a simple principle:

placer mes photos dans mon carnet et me laisser essayer autre chose sans stress

Anything that forces the user to understand the engine’s internal terminology becomes suspect.

The quick workflow simplifies

The modal window is gradually reduced to just a few choices:

  • sorting photos;
  • number of pages;
  • photos per page;
  • margins;
  • spacing;
  • layout: regular, alternating, occasional full-page spreads;
  • Global action: Reorganise all;
  • local action: Reorganise on one page.

The ‘Quick’ and ‘Wizard’ buttons disappear from the header of this modal. Quick mode is now the default mode. The narrative wizard remains in the codebase, but it does not need to be displayed in this workflow until it has a clear product specification.

The main button remains result-oriented:

Placer X photos dans le carnet

This is clearer than “Start auto-fill”.

Global preview: what is seen must be what is applied

The preview becomes the centrepiece of the workflow.

It shows the notebook after simulated filling, without modifying the store until the user applies the changes. It includes existing pages, pages that have been added, the cover where included, and retains the current position when changing style or rhythm.

Several UI details have been refined:

  • the unnecessary preview counter has been removed;
  • the ‘page modified’ borders have been removed;
  • the arrows have been moved closer to the notebook;
  • the controls are grouped on the left;
  • the help section has been transformed into a reassuring, overlay panel;
  • the close button is more visible, without any unnecessary tooltips;
  • the page backgrounds before thumbnails load are replaced by a paper-like grey;
  • the sliders use a terracotta colour consistent with the buttons.

The preview is no longer just for decoration. It serves to reassure users.

Reorganise everything, then just one page

The ‘Reorganise All’ button maintains the selected layout. If the user is set to ‘regular’, it remains in ‘regular’ mode. It changes the compatible templates, not the client’s overall logic.

A major bug has been fixed: with one photo per page, the engine was still forcing full-width display. This was consistent with a previous contract, but contrary to actual usage: if the local ‘Reorganise’ button can suggest other templates for a photo, ‘Reorganise All’ must be able to do so as well.

The cover is given the same trial feature: when it contains a photo, the local ‘Reorganise’ button appears on the front cover, centred on the right-hand half, not in the middle of the spread.

Undo without creating a second editor

The Undo button becomes a mini composition history.

It retains up to 5 states, but only for:

  • ‘Reorganise All’;
  • Reorganise a page.

Manual adjustments such as margins, spacing, rhythm or photos per page reset this history. This is intentional: the aim is to undo a visual exploration, not to create a parallel history system within the modal.

Here again, KISS does not mean a lack of convenience. It is a refusal to add a mechanism whose scope the user would no longer understand.

Local seed: the trust reminder

Today’s work is also marked by the fear of losing locally stored data.

The day before, anti-seed protection was put in place. Today, the issue remains relevant: a local database intended to serve as a mirror must not be treated as a disposable database. The Zine product, visible on the VPS but absent locally, served as a very concrete reminder.

An AI tool can execute a command quickly. The project, however, requires a slow and non-negotiable rule:

ne jamais ecraser silencieusement des donnees metier vivantes

What Day 100 reveals about the project

Code generates quickly. Sometimes too quickly.

In an hour, you can get an auto-fill feature with dozens of parameters. But it then takes two days to organise the semantic and visual chaos: which words to keep, which controls to hide, which preview to trust, which action cancels what, which page is really the target, which option builds trust and which creates confusion.

Day 100 therefore does not mark a major functional expansion. It marks a discipline:

puissance interne, simplicite externe

And that is probably a good definition of KEREDIT at this stage: a ‘workshop-first’ product that must hide a great deal of complexity without deceiving the user.

body.source:
Horaires de session

  • Agent utilisé : Codex
  • Environnement principal : VS Code WSL, plugin Codex, repo local
  • Date couverte : mardi 30 juin 2026
  • Branche KEREDIT observée : dev
  • SHA de fin de séquence observe : d132499 (chore: bump release to 0.9.50)
  • Version KEREDIT observée : 0.9.50
  • Temps minimal observe le 30 juin : 4h24+ d’amplitude de chantier (11:11 -> 15:35)
  • Temps cumulé minimal du bloc 29/30/01 à la fin du 30 juin : 13h29+
  • Temps cumulé minimal depuis le début du journal : environ 603h21+ (598h57+ au 29 juin, + 4h24+ ce jour)

Lecture globale

Le Jour 99 est une journée de garde-fous.

Elle commence par des sujets très techniques : migration pnpm, guardrails Fabric, runtime catalog des templates, refresh retryable. Puis elle bifurque vers un problème beaucoup plus sensible : la base locale ne doit plus être seedée au mauvais moment, surtout quand elle doit servir de miroir au VPS.

La leçon est rude mais utile : une commande de développement qui semblait anodine peut détruire de la confiance produit si elle remplace des données métier attendues.

Tooling et contrats éditeur

Les premiers commits structurent la base technique :

  • d6f1fe1 - migrer le workspace vers pnpm 11 ;
  • ba08cb7 - ajouter des guardrails Fabric ;
  • d16d4bc - documenter le certificat auto-signe Accurio ;
  • 6685ce8 - restaurer une baseline shared book ;
  • 0cb69ff - rafraîchir le runtime catalog de mise en page photo ;
  • 2466fa1 - garder le refresh de layouts retryable.

Ces changements sont moins visibles qu’un panneau UI, mais ils stabilisent les zones ou les régressions coûtent cher : Fabric, les templates runtime, la compatibilité outil, et les intégrations atelier.

Base locale : ne plus confondre seed et miroir

Le commit f94432e est le signal le plus important du jour :

chore: protect local VPS mirror from seed

Le contexte est simple et douloureux : le produit Zine et d’autres données admin existent sur le VPS, mais peuvent disparaître localement si un seed ou un reset traite la base de développement comme un terrain jetable.

Pour KEREDIT, ce n’est plus acceptable. Le local sert parfois de miroir de diagnostic. Il doit donc être protégé contre les commandes destructrices par défaut.

La règle produit est claire :

preserver les donnees admin/metier avant de reconstruire une base

Le seed reste utile pour démarrer une base vierge contrôlée. Il ne doit pas être une réponse automatique à une base déjà vivante.

Panneau Templates : simplifier ce qui se voit

La fin de journée revient à l’UX :

  • 93262cb - compacter le résume de sélection templates ;
  • f3f9a07 - simplifier les détails de sélection ;
  • 1c7b05b - clarifier le texte d’aide ;
  • 468ae1b - compacter le sélecteur nombre de photos ;
  • 8d49c8e - corriger la densité de la grille ;
  • 9001a08 - ajouter une respiration de scrollbar.

Le panneau Templates sert de référence pour le remplissage carnet. Ses contrôles doivent être compréhensibles, cohérents, et suffisamment denses pour travailler vite.

La journée confirme un principe qui va dominer le lendemain :

si une option existe pour le moteur, elle n'a pas forcement a exister pour le client

Ce que cette journée laisse

Le Jour 99 prépare le Jour 100.

D’un cote, les garde-fous techniques protègent le socle : pnpm, Fabric, runtime catalog, seed local. De l’autre, les panneaux commencent a être tailles pour l’usage réel, pas pour montrer toutes les possibilités du moteur.

La suite logique est évidente : reprendre le remplissage carnet avec le même état d’esprit. Garder la puissance interne, mais retirer le bruit visible.

Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin, KEREDIT repository and GOF repository
  • Date covered: Monday 29 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch observed: dev
  • KEREDIT SHA at the end of the observed sequence: e1d5676 (fix(woocommerce): compact resume project chooser)
  • KEREDIT version observed: 0.9.47
  • GOF branch observed: dev
  • GOF SHA at the end of the sequence observed: 37b38da (fix(ui): enlarge GOF favicon text)
  • GOF version observed in today’s history: 0.1.85, then most recent local repository at 0.1.86
  • Minimum duration observed on 29 June: 9h05+ of works duration (09:27 -> 18:32 KEREDIT; GOF 12:08 -> 16:51, included in the same window)
  • Minimum cumulative time for block 29/30/01 as at the end of 29 June: 9h05+
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 598h57+ (589h52+ as at 28 June, + 9h05+ today)

Overall summary

Today’s work moves away slightly from the visible core of the editor to strengthen the tools surrounding it.

The photo log is still present with the ‘refill’ preview, but the main thread is now up and running: reducing noise, making feed testing easier, documenting upcoming editor projects, and hardening GOF in terms of security and performance.

It’s not the sort of day that yields a spectacular screenshot. It’s the sort of day that prevents the beta from becoming impossible to monitor.

KEREDIT: refill, lint and workshop command

Today’s KEREDIT commits:

  • 0aa6b31 - aligning the notebook refill preview;
  • 87d667d - restore a clean lint state;
  • a513692 - track the editor refactoring backlog;
  • 7051e75 - reduce beta observability noise;
  • a59e3a2 - added the `test-flux` command for the workshop pipeline;
  • 30ea669 - bump release 0.9.47;
  • e1d5676 - streamline the WooCommerce project recovery options.

The most important practical point is test-flux. A workshop pipeline cannot rely solely on unit tests or manual clicks. We need a command capable of replaying the WooCommerce -> KEREDIT -> GOF -> workshop flow in a reproducible manner.

The other useful point is the reduction in observability noise. Too many logs make the real signals invisible. In closed beta, we want to see the errors that change a decision, not every single system heartbeat.

WooCommerce: resuming without overloading

The WooCommerce project resumption selector has been streamlined.

This is not a cosmetic detail. In the e-commerce workflow, users often return after an interruption: an order link, a project already created, photos already present, and a decision to resume. If the resumption screen looks like a technical dashboard, trust declines.

The fix follows the same principle as the order form: less mental load, a clearer path.

GOF: security, cache and staging retention

GOF also saw significant changes that day:

  • f1341a8 - tightening access to artefacts and rendering;
  • 61e98a6 - limiting the cache buffer for PDF assets;
  • 43fdfff /e7bc345 - adding and then tightening the staging retention workflow;
  • 7adff60 - released GOF 0.1.85;
  • e38bf59 / 37b38da - added and then enlarged the GOF favicon.

The GOF hardening counts towards KEREDIT because GOF is not an annex. It is the artefacts forge: web PDFs, print PDFs, workshop files, operator verification. If GOF retains data for too long, exposes too much, or consumes too much cache space, the entire chain becomes vulnerable.

What this day leaves us with

The theme of the day is simple:

moins de bruit -> plus de diagnostic
plus de replay -> moins de superstition

KEREDIT is starting to have the tools needed to test an entire workshop workflow without having to mentally reconstruct everything every time an incident occurs. GOF is becoming stricter on security and more resource-efficient.

It’s not spectacular, but it’s exactly the sort of work that makes a beta version usable.

  • Date covered: Sunday 28 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch observed: dev following the merge of the templates project
  • SHA at the end of the observed sequence: af85675 (fix(editor): align autofill preview and empty slots)
  • KEREDIT version observed: 0.9.45
  • Time windows observed: 00:40:11 → 01:00:43, 09:41:39 → 10:00:14, then 17:23:56 → 19:09:30 CEST
  • Minimum observed duration: approximately 2h25+, conservative sum of the three blocks
  • Minimum cumulative duration since the start of the log: approximately 589h52+ (587h27+ as at 27 June, + 2h25+ today)

Overall reading

Sunday begins as a logical extension of 27 June: whilst the logbook can be filled in using templates, it can also be accompanied by a narrative intent.

But the day soon reveals a tension that will become central in the days that follow: adding functions is easy; organising their meaning is much more difficult.

The narrative assistant arrives. The templates are enhanced. Then the work immediately returns to something more down-to-earth: stabilising the hooks, making the preview reliable, aligning empty slots, and ensuring that the pop-up form doesn’t become an incomprehensible control panel.

Narrative assistant and enhanced templates

The first commits of the night set out an ambition:

  • f16e21c - to enhance the photo layout templates;
  • 911cebe - to add a narrative assistant for photo books;
  • 64449ca - clean up the content of the narrative assistant.

It’s a powerful idea: a photo book isn’t just a pile of images. It can have a rhythm, pauses, captions and a logical sequence.

But the risk is just as clear. If the wizard, the templates, the styles and the auto-fill each speak their own language, the user doesn’t save any time. They end up with added complexity.

Stabilise before expanding

The rest of the day’s discussion brings the topic back to the product level:

  • ac3e6f2 - keeping the hooks in the auto-fill modal stable;
  • b5b8581 - implement Impeccable and refine the autocomplete modal;
  • af85675 - align the autocomplete preview with the empty fields;
  • 0089b32 - release version 0.9.45.

The crucial point is the preview. A fill preview cannot be merely decorative. If it does not show the actual project, with the correct pages, the correct placements and the correct boundaries, it is misleading.

Automatic layout is therefore beginning to move beyond a simple form. It must become a visual experience: seeing the notebook, understanding what is going to be added, and being able to try a different layout.

What this day corrects in the method

The risk of over-engineering is already apparent.

There are enough building blocks to construct a powerful workflow:

  • narrative assistant;
  • templates;
  • sorting;
  • pacing;
  • number of photos per page;
  • preview;
  • filling;
  • reuse at a later stage.

But too many building blocks on display in one place create confusion. Today’s work already points in a direction that will be confirmed later: quick mode must remain quick. Technical concepts may exist in the code, but they must not all become visible options.

What this day leaves us with

The photo log is starting to take shape around two main themes:

composition automatique -> poser les photos
assistant narratif      -> proposer une lecture

These two strands are useful, but they must not be mixed too soon. The product needs internal power and external simplicity. Moving forward, the focus should be less on adding options and more on choosing which ones to hide.

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin, local repository
  • Date covered: Saturday 27 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch observed: dev / UI editor projects
  • SHA at the end of the observed sequence: 488eb52 (feat(editor): persist photo layout templates)
  • KEREDIT version: 0.9.44/0.9.45 depending on the subsequent merge sequence; not recalculated to the nearest commit
  • Observed windows: 00:16:40 → 00:48:42, then 16:30:09 → 23:11:52 CEST
  • Minimum observed time: approximately 7h13+, a conservative sum of the two blocks excluding the long outage
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 587h27+ (580h14+ as at 26 June, + 7h13+ today)

Overall summary

The previous day had separated two topics that tended to get mixed up too easily: the web PDF on the one hand, the workshop print on the other. Today we return to the editor, but with the same underlying idea: a visual interface is not enough; a contract is needed.

For photo albums, the contract is beginning to take the form of templates. A template is not just a pretty layout. It is a reusable rule that specifies how many photos a page can hold, or where they fall, how a page responds to the chosen number of photos, and how automatic filling can offer something other than a bare grid.

Autofill is therefore evolving into a layout language, not just a magic button.

What has been built

Today’s commits show a fairly clear progression:

  • a1beea2 - simplifying a group of shape layers;
  • 7110d73 - adding canvas/page navigation arrows;
  • ac7c69e - widening the controls at the bottom of the editor;
  • 9e1f4bd - clarifying the page navigation controls;
  • 49331f7 - clarifying the spine and cover guides in books;
  • 3dfdd38 - add photo layout templates for books;
  • d91b738 - add sorting and spacing to auto-fill;
  • e057667 - add ‘full photo’ templates;
  • 42cbaee - make photo layout settings live;
  • 488eb52 - save photo layout templates.

The key point is the shift from static to interactive: layouts are no longer simply coded as arbitrary positions; they can now be selected, varied and saved.

Covers, double-page spreads and limits

The book project also continues to highlight that a book is not a homogeneous sequence of ordinary pages.

The front cover, inside front cover, inside back cover, spine and the pages of the inner section do not all serve the same purpose. Navigation must therefore remain clear: you can view a double-page spread, but certain areas are not editable and certain zones belong to the cover as a whole rather than to the inner section.

The guidelines for the spine and cover have been clarified to avoid a simple but dangerous misunderstanding: believing that what is visible on screen necessarily corresponds to a customer-editable page.

Autofill: the first true logic

Autofill now has two functions:

  • photo sorting;
  • page layout.

This is still a work in progress, not a final UX. But the principle is established: the client should not have to compose each page by hand to achieve a coherent album, nor should the tool impose a monotonous grid.

The “full-photo” templates add a much-needed sense of breathing space. A photo book needs dense pages, but also pages that allow a single image to stand on its own.

What this day reveals

The day highlights a clear product direction:

photos chargees -> tri -> rythme -> gabarits -> proposition de carnet

There is still a lot of UX work to be done. But the technical foundation is starting to speak the right language. Auto-fill must not be a black box; it must be a suggestion that the user can understand, modify, and dismiss without losing their flow.
