body.source:
Post prepared during the live tests on Wednesday 10 June 2026. The status described here corresponds to the code pushed and deployed up to KEREDIT 0.6.102.

Session times

  • Agent used: Codex
  • Environments observed: Krampouz/KEREDIT at dépôt local krampouz, GOF at dépôt local gof, KEREDIT VPS, WordPress/WooCommerce live
  • Date: Wednesday 10 June 2026
  • KEREDIT development/deployment branch: dev
  • KEREDIT SHA at the end of the live sequence: 4efe897
  • KEREDIT version at the end of the live sequence: 0.6.102
  • GOF branch observed: dev
  • Observed GOF SHA: 4249b81
  • Observed KEREDIT commit amplitude: 11:15 -> 18:45
  • Observed GOF commit amplitude: 11:16
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 445h54+

Brief conclusion

The day began with a contractual issue: why do the KEREDIT publisher, the transmitted JSON, GOF and the PDF still diverge when the fields appear to exist somewhere?

It ended with another, more business-related issue: a template can no longer be thought of as a single layout that is stretched across different formats. A template becomes an editorial family, with a variant for each format, and the client can switch from 10x15 to 10x10 without losing the photo that has already been placed.

In between, we also fixed a TLS security issue, made the photo placeholder sharper, and then traced several live bugs from WordPress to WooCommerce to KEREDIT back to their true source: not the plugin itself, but the continuity between template variants, created projects, client permissions, format changes and client content.

Morning: auditing the KEREDIT → GOF JSON contract

The first KEREDIT commit of the day, 298cde9, carries out a full audit of the KEREDIT → GOF JSON contract.

This work stems from a painful but useful realisation: guessing field by field is no longer enough. Image, text, clipart and shape blocks must have an explicit decision regarding:

  • field to be persisted and rendered;
  • field deliberately ignored;
  • field not supported but deferred;
  • field missing from the payload and therefore requiring correction.

The audit adds traceable documentation to docs/audits/keredit-gof-json-contract-2026-06-10.md, strengthens the backend tests for the export payload and verifies that important fields survive all the way to KereditPdfForgePayloadV1.pages.

On the GOF side, 4249b81 implements the same logic: the renderer is better equipped to audit KEREDIT canvas fields, and the fixtures for the sensitive commands 1075752 and 1075753 act as safeguards.

The method point is important: when the editor and the PDF do not match, the problem must be treated as a contract bug, not as a blind rendering tweak.

Security: remove the GOF TLS bypass

The commit 8feb9ef fixes a targeted security issue in the KEREDIT-side GOF client.

The GOF configuration helper was disabling TLS validation via rejectUnauthorized: false. Even though the current live configuration uses a GOF HTTP LAN, this flaw posed a risk to any future HTTPS instances: GOF bearer tokens, the Accurio catalogue and cached responses must not pass through a channel that silently accepts an invalid certificate.

The fix is deliberately minimal:

  • removal of the unconditional TLS bypass;
  • addition of a check to prevent its silent reintroduction;
  • retaining the current HTTP LAN behaviour;
  • no new global bypass flag.

The result is more robust: if an HTTPS GOF has a faulty certificate, the certificate will need to be fixed, not KEREDIT weakened.

Placeholder photo: sharper first impression

The commit ea77ae1, followed by part of ac5e85f, address a very noticeable issue: the empty photo placeholder.

Before the fix, the icon and the text “Add a photo” could appear blurry or become out of sync with the frame during interactions. This isn’t just an aesthetic issue: it’s the first thing a customer sees before adding their photo.

The placeholder rendering now remains vector-based, rather than being cached as a blurry bitmap, and its sub-elements are tagged to follow the frame during resizing and dragging:

  • placeholder background;
  • icon;
  • labelling;
  • block border.

The `test:photo-placeholder` test locks in this behaviour. The aim is simple: even before the client-side image loads, the slot must look clean.

The real challenge: multi-format templates

The commit 3bbe914 switches the template model.

The old implicit approach was too limited: a template had a pages_data, and then that layout was adapted to another format. This works for simple cases, but it doesn’t reflect the business requirements. A 10x15, a 10x10, a 13x18 or a 20x20 may require different layouts.

The new template introduces TemplateFormatVariant:

  • template_id ;
  • the name and dimensions of the format;
  • pages_data specific to that format;
  • a thumbnail, if applicable;
  • is_default marker.

Template.pages_data Compatibility remains temporary, but the variants become the nominal source. The builder knows how to load the exact variant, create a new one by adapting it when it does not exist, and then save only the variant for the current format.

Creating a standard project from a template follows the same rule: the exact variant if available, otherwise adaptation from the default variant.

WordPress -> WooCommerce -> KEREDIT: following the actual path

Live tests subsequently showed that the front end was not synchronised with the variants, even though they had been saved.

The first instinct might have been to blame the WordPress plugin. However, the logs revealed something else:

  • WordPress was indeed sending template_id;
  • it was also sending the format requested within the KEREDIT context;
  • the backend was creating a project linked to the correct template;
  • but some paths were still reading Template.pages_data or adapting the pages locally.

The commit ac5e85f fixes project creation from the WooCommerce launch. backend/src/services/woocommerce-service.ts now resolves template pages via TemplateFormatVariant, exactly like the standard project route.

The actual integration test verifies that a WooCommerce launch using a template utilises the exact variant, not the old legacy pages_data.

The next pitfall: changing the format in the client editor

Once the Woo creation had been corrected, another discrepancy appeared in the editor.

The project was indeed derived from the template, but the frontend did not retain enough information to recognise that a format change required the exact variant. It simply did:

pages courantes -> adaptPagesToFormat(...)

The commit 7469656 therefore adds the minimum necessary logic: a project generated from a template retains its sourceTemplateId on the store editor side. When the client changes the format, RightPanel calls the API /templates/:id with the target format.

If the API returns variant_source: "exact", the publisher applies this variant. Otherwise, it retains the existing adaptive fallback.

This fix has resolved the main bug visible in production: switching to the 10x10 format now finally loads the 10x10 layout saved in the builder, rather than stretching the 10x15 layout.

The overlooked issue: retaining the client’s photo

The final discovery of the day is the most business-specific.

Yes, the layout must change when switching from 10x15 to 10x10. But if the client has already placed a photo in the slot, that photo must not disappear. The target variant must replace the composition, not reset the project to blank.

The commit e041449 adds this merge:

  • the target variant provides the block’s geometry, position and permissions;
  • the current project provides the client content that has already been placed;
  • for a photo block of the same id, KEREDIT retains the assetId, original aspect ratio, crop, pan, zoom, internal rotation, flip and image enhancements;
  • for a text block with the same ‘id’, KEREDIT preserves the rich text content.

The test:template-format-variant test explicitly verifies this scenario: a 10x10 variant with an empty placeholder retrieves the client’s photo placed at 10x15, whilst retaining the geometry 10x10.

This is probably the most important product rule of the day: variants drive the design, but the project drives the client’s work.

The contradiction in template permissions

Following the multi-format deployment, a very specific bug emerged on the product Carte postale, using the Postal theme: on 10x15, the block correctly displayed “Add a photo”, but the client was unable to drag and drop a photo into it. Switching to other formats seemed to restore normal behaviour.

The cause was neither a drag-and-drop issue nor a WooCommerce issue. The template contained two contradictory messages:

  • the image block was an empty, editable and unlocked placeholder;
  • the template’s global permissions prohibited ‘canReplaceAsset’.

The front end therefore adhered to the global permission and silently refused the replacement, whilst the interface promised a usable photo slot.

The commits 0052ab0 and afcd1d3 resolve this issue. On the backend, a project derived from a template can no longer be published with an empty, editable but non-replaceable photo block. The rule applies to standard project creation, to creation via the WooCommerce launch screen, and to project saving, to prevent an already open tab from reverting to the previous state via autosave.

The live data has also been corrected for tpl_postcard_postal: the template has reverted to consistent client permissions, and the affected draft has been restored to canReplaceAsset: true without reopening the other actions.

Replacing a photo should be a natural action

Last UX tweak of the day: once an image block already contains a photo, the client must be able to replace it without deleting the block, without recreating a layout and without losing the frame.

The commit 4efe897 adds this behaviour:

  • dragging a photo onto an empty block: immediate placement;
  • dropping a photo onto a block that is already filled: “Replace the photo?” confirmation;
  • clicking on a photo whilst an image block is selected: same confirmation;
  • same photo as the one already present: no action;
  • non-replaceable block: no action, no silent behaviour, no addition elsewhere.

After confirmation, KEREDIT retains the block’s geometry: position, size, rotation, permissions, mask and decorative frame. However, the new photo starts afresh in ‘cover’ mode, with cropping, panning, zooming, internal rotation and image enhancements reset to zero. This is the right balance for a customer service solution: the block remains the editorial container, whilst the replaced photo starts from a readable state.

Documentation and observability

Two documentation commits accompanied the day’s work:

  • 1eaa675 implements a beta observability design centred on OpenReplay and VictoriaMetrics;
  • 143cfee adds an implementation plan.

The commit bc466d7 also updates AGENTS.md, BIBLIOTHEQUE.md, docs/HOME.md and CHANGELOG.md with the new multi-format contract.

This documentation is useful because the subject is subtle: it is no longer enough to simply say “adapt the pages to the format”. Three things must be distinguished:

  • exact template variant;
  • adaptive fallback;
  • merging of client-side content already entered.

Deployments and validations

It was a very action-packed day. The KEREDIT versions have progressed to 0.6.102, with several short VPS deployments.

Notable checks covered:

  • pnpm --filter backend typecheck ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend typecheck ;
  • pnpm --filter backend test -- src/real-db.integration.test.ts ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend test:photo-placeholder ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend test:photo-block ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend test:template-format-variant ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend test:image-clipart-helpers ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend test:asset-builders ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend exec tsx ./tests/photoReplacement.test.ts ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend lint, with the pre-existing warning on TextFrameEditor;
  • pnpm build ;
  • VPS smoke checks;
  • public health check for https://ooblik.keredit.com/api/health.

The live version observed at the end of the sequence is 0.6.102, SHA 4efe8970d5f4, with both backend and frontend in a healthy state.

Closure decision

The day has reinforced an important product strategy: KEREDIT cannot simply be a publisher that adapts rectangles. It must retain a business purpose.

For multi-format templates, this focus is now clearer:

  • the design team can prepare a layout for each format;
  • the client can change the format within the same product;
  • the project retrieves the exact variant where one exists;
  • content already added by the client survives the change.

This is not merely a convenience feature. It is what makes changing formats commercially viable: the client can explore another format without feeling that KEREDIT is taking away their work.

A point to bear in mind for the future: this logic must remain valid beyond the simple photo block. Rich text, recoloured clipart, frames and masks must follow the same philosophy: a variant for the layout, a project for the client’s content.

Another point to bear in mind: each permission template must be conceived as an interface promise. If the screen says ‘Add a photo’, the project contract must make this action possible. Otherwise, the client will see it as a bug, even if technically the code ‘complies’ with a permission.

description.source: Audit of the KEREDIT-GOF JSON contract, TLS hardening, photo placeholder, live stabilisation of multi-format templates and seamless photo replacement in image blocks.

body.source:
Post finalised following GOF correction 0.1.49 regarding the image mismatch between the KEREDIT JSON and the GOF PDF output.

Session times

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Environments observed: Krampouz/KEREDIT at dépôt local krampouz, GOF at dépôt local gof
  • Date: Tuesday 9 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch: dev
  • KEREDIT SHA observed at the time of writing: fbfbd09
  • KEREDIT version observed: 0.6.92
  • GOF branch: dev
  • GOF version observed after correction: 0.1.49
  • GOF SHA observed after correction: 347a563
  • Time span observed across KEREDIT commits: 08:23 -> 19:14
  • Duration observed via GOF commits: 19:16 -> 19:33
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 438h24+

Brief conclusion

The day began with efforts to make the editor more visually credible: improved preview resolution, a configurable splash image, better-loaded original photos, a sharper adaptive grid, followed by smoother panning and scrolling within the canvas.

The focus then shifted to a more product-related issue: WooCommerce client projects need to be handled with greater care. A project that has already been commissioned must not be re-edited as an open draft; duplication is now the standard procedure for resuming work without compromising the order history.

The end of the day wrapped up the trickiest issue: image alignment between KEREDIT and GOF. KEREDIT had strengthened its rendering freshness contract; GOF 0.1.49 can now render KEREDIT’s image adjustments with the correct rotation origin and the same direction of rotation as the editor.

This morning: making the editor look sharper

The main focus of the day was very clear: the editor had to stop looking blurry or flimsy as soon as you looked at a real photo.

The reference commits on the KEREDIT side show the progress:

  • a569076 adds a configurable splash screen;
  • 89c395e adds configurable effects to this screen;
  • 411039c increases the resolution of the editor previews;
  • b6962fe then 67e32f2 makes the launch preview image more reliable;
  • 8402bf3 improves the comfort zoom in the Postcard editor.

This isn’t just a cosmetic update. In the beta, the user needs to understand that they are working on a printable object, not a rough thumbnail. The zoom function, sharpness, loading time and stability of the canvas are all key to building trust in the product.

Photos: keep the original as the definitive version, speed up the display

The major technical overhaul of the image handling then resumed the previously documented approach: the original remains the production standard, whilst the adaptive raster remains a temporary on-screen cache.

KEREDIT now loads original photos more efficiently into the canvas (44905a2), keeps photos attached whilst dragging (272fd34 / 35d99e6), makes adaptive rasters sharper (be46fcf), maintains their correct fit (7881b03), and then defers computationally intensive tasks so as not to block user interactions (5eb7146).

The key point is the trade-off: the editor must respond immediately when a photo is moved or resized, but it must not sacrifice the quality of the exported output. The day therefore further clarified the division of responsibilities:

  • rapid on-screen feedback during interaction;
  • a browser cache to avoid re-reading the original with every action;
  • a persistent contract that continues to refer to the source image, not the cache.

Overlays and editor gestures

The commit b865919 refines overlay interactions. This is consistent with the rest of the day’s work: now that images are larger and sharper, we must ensure that guides, selections and toolbars do not give the impression of being pasted on or lagging behind.

This work remains within the beta track: we won’t reopen the stable typography branch, but we’ll remove visible friction around image manipulation.

WooCommerce: resuming the order without breaking it

The other half of the day focused on the customer journey and the WooCommerce plugin.

The commit 854f288 imposes a precautionary rule: a project that has already been ordered must be duplicated before it can be resumed. This is an important business requirement. An order placed constitutes a commercial and production record; reopening it as an editable draft would be dangerous.

The next set of changes improves the user experience:

  • 281d7ac loads client projects progressively;
  • c379067 simplifies validation checks;
  • 456b5c4 clarifies bulk selection;
  • fbfbd09 refines batch actions.

The expected outcome for clients is simpler: finding their projects, understanding which ones have been commissioned, duplicating them when they need to start again, and avoiding ambiguous actions.

Bug fixed: KEREDIT and GOF are reading the same image contract

The end of the day was the point of tension.

KEREDIT has an explicit commit, ‘0beb905’ (Fix image render contract freshness), which affects page validation, the GOF payload, PDF/print job routes, PDF administration and project persistence. The message is clear: the image rendering contract needed to be updated and made more explicit before renderings were sent or reused.

On the GOF side, the fix was carried out in three stages:

  • 9f33865 (Render Keredit image adjustments in GOF) adds the rendering of KEREDIT image adjustments in app/src/pdf-renderer.js with an associated test;
  • 7756fb5 (Fix GOF image block rotation origin) corrects the rotation origin of the image blocks;
  • 347a563 (Mirror editor image rotation in GOF PDFs) aligns the GOF rotation direction with that of the editor.

The bug was therefore not simply a visual difference in the PDF. It was a contract bug between:

  • the editor’s persistent JSON;
  • the payload exported by KEREDIT;
  • the GOF interpretation;
  • the final PDF rendering.

GOF0.1.49 documents the resolution of this issue: KEREDIT image adjustments, the rotation origin and the direction of rotation are now rendered on the same side of the string.

Closure decision

The day ends on a better note than it began: the image editor is now more user-friendly, the WooCommerce project workflow is less fraught, and the KEREDIT → GOF bridge resolves a specific discrepancy between JSON and PDF.

Point to bear in mind for the future: whenever a PDF rendering does not match the editor, the correct approach remains to follow the full contract rather than patching the final rendering based on intuition. The pipeline must be checked in this order: persistent JSON, exported payload, GOF interpretation, generated PDF.

description.source: Improvements to image rendering in the editor, improved zoom functionality, more conservative WooCommerce projects, followed by the GOF 0.1.49 fix for the KEREDIT JSON contract/image rendering.

body.source:
Session timetable

  • System used: Codex
  • Date: Monday 8 June 2026.
  • Environments: Krampouz/KEREDIT at dépôt local krampouz, GOF at dépôt local gof, KEREDIT VPS.
  • KEREDIT branch: dev.
  • End-of-day KEREDIT SHA: 6eeb30a.
  • End-of-day KEREDIT version: 0.6.78.
  • GOF SHA observed at the end of the day: 6c9ffd7.
  • KEREDIT commit amplitude: 08:59 -> 17:49.
  • GOF commit amplitude: 10:36 -> 18:15.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 427h14+.

Brief conclusion

8 June marked the milestone for the ‘friends and family’ beta. The day was not about opening things up widely. Rather, it tightened the security measures: more recoverable publisher access, a more robust splash screen, a protected WooCommerce webhook, a written security audit, and, above all, a much stricter PDF contract between KEREDIT and GOF.

The practical conclusion is a cautious one: the beta can move forward, but not whilst leaving grey areas in order flows, webhooks or PDFs.

The editor login must allow users to log back in

The morning begins with ‘2b719d8’: the editor’s launch screen must allow users to log in again. This point stems from a very real scenario: a user might arrive from WooCommerce, have an expired session, or encounter an intermediate state during launch.

The previous behaviour could leave the user facing a splash screen that simply waits, with no clear course of action. The fix adds a cleaner exit:

  • the splash screen now distinguishes more clearly between waiting, error and re-login;
  • ProtectedRoute and the application bootstrap works more seamlessly;
  • the wording avoids mentioning unnecessary technical details;
  • the package versions are aligned for deployment.

Reference commit: 2b719d8 (fix: allow reconnect from editor launch splash).

Splash: making recovery more robust, not just improving the appearance

The commit f99b27e continues this work with a more comprehensive hardening of recovery. The application receives a proper RouteErrorBoundary, the bootstrap becomes more explicit, and the launch store better preserves the state required to handle errors.

This is a trust-building fix: a beta version cannot expect a user to understand whether a frozen screen is caused by a session, a frontend chunk, a route, or a WooCommerce launch. It must offer a simple action: reload, log in again, or resume.

Security: the WooCommerce webhook must not be public

The commit 48f5f1d is today’s most visible security measure: the WooCommerce webhook now requires a key. This is no minor detail. A webhook route that accepts order events must be authenticated, even in a closed beta.

The fix:

  • removes the dangerous default resolution on the credentials side;
  • enforces a webhook key at the endpoint;
  • adds integration tests;
  • documents the behaviour in the plugin guide;
  • writes the ‘docs/audits/2026-06-08-audit-securite-beta-publique.md’ audit.

The message is simple: testing can be carried out with a small number of clients, but public endpoints must not be left open simply for convenience.

Reference commit: 48f5f1d (fix(security): require WooCommerce webhook key).

PDF text: the contract becomes stricter

The biggest technical task of the day is still the text. 7 June established the contract; 8 June made it stricter.

KEREDIT first added c23432a, a clearer documentation of the KEREDIT-GOF text contract. Then d4616fb locks this contract on the backend:

  • stricter page validation;
  • text field diagnostics;
  • enriched export payload;
  • updated JSON project schema;
  • tests on the validator and the payload.

Nextaa22062, issues a strict text layout contract in the PDF export. shared/src/utils/richText.ts sets out the standardisation more clearly, and the rich text tests cover cases that should no longer depend on local interpretations.

Finally, 6eeb30a explicitly declares the PDF font synthesis policy. This is a subtle but important point: if the system synthesises italics or bold text due to the lack of an exact variant, this must be a decision visible in the contract, not a hidden behaviour of the rendering engine.

Reference commits:

  • c23432a (docs: verrouiller le contrat texte KEREDIT GOF) ;
  • d4616fb (fix(pdf): verrouille le contrat texte GOF) ;
  • aa22062 (fix: emit strict PDF text layout contract) ;
  • 6eeb30a (fix: declare PDF font synthesis policy).

GOF: from glyph to regression guardrail

GOF is progressing at the same pace:

  • b0b16ca corrects the deterministic rendering of ligatures;
  • ebfdfcc fixes text shaping at the glyph level;
  • 0df3422 adds text contraction diagnostics;
  • 526e221 displays the bleed guide in the PDF preview;
  • f6688c3 and dd778fc adds PDF download and command-linked filenames;
  • f9e49c1 applies the KEREDIT text layout contract;
  • c98d3f4 synthesises italics for exact variants;
  • 2de371b maintains the compact line height of rich text;
  • 4d9d48b includes the renderer version in job reuse;
  • 6c9ffd7 documents PDF regression safeguards.

It is no longer simply a matter of ‘creating a PDF’. It is about making the PDF inspectable, downloadable, versioned, and sufficiently deterministic to enable comparison between the screen preview and the final output.

The 8 June beta becomes a controlled launch

The production notes already stated that 8 June was to remain a limited release for selected clients, not a wide-scale launch. Today’s work confirms this approach.

What has been reinforced:

  • a more reliable editor launch;
  • a secure WooCommerce webhook;
  • written beta security audit;
  • PDF contract text documented and tested;
  • GOF better equipped to diagnose rendering discrepancies;
  • 0.6.78 of the advanced KEREDIT version.

What has not yet been given the all-clear:

  • each Woo -> editor -> basket path must continue to be tested in a real product context;
  • projects opened outside the product sheet may exist, but must not be confused with orderable projects;
  • PDFs must continue to be compared using realistic text examples;
  • customer messages must remain understandable without technical jargon.

What is solid this evening

  • KEREDIT ends the day at 6eeb30a, version 0.6.78.
  • The WooCommerce webhook is protected by a key.
  • The public beta security audit of 8 June has been documented.
  • The editor launch splash screen now displays cleaner output.
  • The PDF text contract is more rigorous, documented and shared.
  • GOF adds diagnostics, bleed previews, PDF downloads and regression safeguards.

What remains to be monitored

The danger is no longer just the obvious bug. It lies in the intermediate states: an expired session, a project resumed from ‘My Projects’, a PDF file reused when the renderer has changed, the exact font missing, or a misconfigured webhook. Today’s session has reduced these grey areas, but it also shows that the beta still requires ongoing support.

The right approach remains: few clients, real-world workflows, and careful verification of the transitions between WooCommerce, KEREDIT, GOF and the workshop.

description.source: Re-establishment of publisher connections, tightening of WooCommerce security, public beta audit and strict enforcement of the PDF contract between KEREDIT and GOF.

title.source: Day 78 – Lock down the beta before scaling up

items.title: Day 78 – Lock down the beta before scaling up

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Software used: Codex
  • Date: Sunday 7 June 2026.
  • Environments: Krampouz/KEREDIT at dépôt local krampouz, GOF at dépôt local gof.
  • KEREDIT branch: dev.
  • End-of-day KEREDIT SHA: be785d6.
  • End-of-day KEREDIT version: 0.6.75.
  • GOF SHA observed at the end of the day: c66e826.
  • KEREDIT commit amplitude: 10:10 -> 20:03.
  • GOF commit amplitude: 10:33 -> 20:15.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 417h58+.

Brief conclusion

The day centred on a topic that may seem narrow but which affects the entire workflow: the text. As long as the publisher, the JSON project, the local PDF and GOF do not speak exactly the same typographical language, a postcard may look good on screen but turn out poorly in production.

So, on 7 June, the text moved from being an editor’s representation to a production contract. Rich text becomes the canonical source, internal text margins are explicitly defined, the old ‘styleRanges’ no longer control the rendering when rich content exists, and GOF learns not to retain obsolete renderings as if they were still current.

Morning: fine-tuning the entry, then holding the zoom

The first commit of the day (0d33377) follows on from 6 June: the editor’s launch screen has been visually tweaked. It’s not the day’s major task, but it’s the gateway the client sees when they switch from WooCommerce to KEREDIT.

The first real functional milestone comes next with ef2aa47: keeping the text stable whilst zooming in the editor. This is a classic issue with a canvas: if resizing, calculated dimensions and live editing do not follow the same logic, the text can shift, change size or appear to float.

The fix affects:

  • EditorCanvas.tsx ;
  • TextFrameEditor.tsx ;
  • useCanvasDimensions.ts ;
  • text frame helpers;
  • a dedicated test for canvas dimensions.

This work is important for the beta: the customer must not feel that their text is changing when they zoom in to inspect it.

WooCommerce: duplicating without losing the basket context

The commit 9adc98c addresses a specific scenario: when a client project that has already been ordered is duplicated, the copy must become editable again, but it must not lose the WooCommerce metadata that allows us to understand where it came from.

The fix adds a real integration test and preserves:

  • wc_product_id ;
  • wc_variation_id ;
  • wc_context_fingerprint ;
  • wc_context.

The aim is not to silently recommend the same project. It is to enable clean duplication: a new draft on the KEREDIT side, with the commercial context still readable on the WooCommerce side.

Reference commit: 9adc98c (fix: preserve Woo metadata on customer duplicates).

Rich text becomes the PDF truth

The major KEREDIT pivot is 2b47806: rich text becomes the canonical contract for the PDF. Until now, the old model styleRanges could still act as a competing ‘truth’. This is dangerous: two representations of the same text always end up diverging.

Today’s decision is clear:

  • if `richText` exists, it controls the rendering;
  • the backend routes normalise and validate this contract;
  • PDF exports convey this truth;
  • the architecture documentation no longer suggests that several equivalent models coexist.

The tests cover the page validator, the export payload and the relevant rendering paths. It’s less spectacular than a new interface, but it’s more valuable: it’s the sort of decision that prevents incorrect PDFs from being produced.

Reference commit: 2b47806 (fix: make rich text the canonical PDF contract).

GOF is following suit

At the same time, GOF is receiving a series of closely related fixes:

  • 0a89b70 renders styled rich text runs correctly in PDFs;
  • f4f8d8e fully embeds print fonts;
  • 31401c1 aligns GOF’s rich text rendering with the KEREDIT specification;
  • 4028077 adds text geometry diagnostics;
  • c4487d9 ignores ‘styleRanges’ metadata when ‘richText’ is canonical;
  • f0e16b6 aligns text insets with the KEREDIT contract.

The chain becomes more consistent: KEREDIT cannot simply export clean JSON; GOF must read it using the same physical conventions.

Duplicate GOF renderings no longer obscure the text

Another production issue: obsolete GOF renderings must not remain visible as if they were still validated. The GOF commits 0bf1f43, 68865a1, 1afa8b5 and c66e826 define the concepts of current rendering, revision and supersede.

The expected outcome is straightforward for the operator: a project must have a readable current version, with its history behind it, not a pile of competing PDFs that forces one to guess which one to send.

This is a key workshop topic. The correct version of the PDF must be obvious.

In the evening: aligning the contract text with the payload

Today’s final KEREDIT commit (be785d6) brings everything together: backend validation, PDF renderer, export payload, management routes, asset routes, WooCommerce, docs, frontend helpers, Fabric object factory, shared types and text layout utilities.

In particular, this commit adds shared/src/utils/textLayout.ts and its tests. It transforms the text into a shared calculation rather than an implicit convention specific to a particular screen.

What’s stable tonight

  • KEREDIT ends the day at be785d6, version 0.6.75.
  • Rich text is the canonical source for the PDF contract.
  • Legacy styleRanges files must no longer contradict rich content.
  • The text remains more stable during editor zooming.
  • GOF now renders styles, fonts, insets and rendering revisions more accurately.
  • Duplicating a commissioned Woo project retains the relevant commercial context.

What remains problematic

The text issue is not yet resolved. The contract has been finalised, but each engine retains its pitfalls: Fabric on-screen, local PDFs, GOF, font embedding, ligatures, line-height, insets, and font substitution. The right approach is not to add more typographical options; it is to continue comparing screen, JSON and PDF outputs using simple but rigorous test cases.

The beta is progressing, but it is now moving forward with a more mature requirement: what the client sees must become what the production environment produces.

description.source: Text stabilisation whilst zooming, rich text normalisation for PDFs, more secure WooCommerce duplication, and KEREDIT-GOF alignment with regard to typographic rendering.

title.source: Day 77 – The text becomes a production contract

items.title: Day 77 – The text becomes a production contract

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Date: Saturday 6 June 2026.
  • Provider: Codex.
  • Environments: Krampouz/KEREDIT, WordPress/WooCommerce connector, KEREDIT VPS, Woo test site.
  • Source branch: dev.
  • Source status at the end of the day: e64994f, application version 0.6.70.
  • KEREDIT WordPress plugin: 0.1.34, private manifest aligned with updates.ooblik.com.
  • Application VPS checked during the day: version 0.6.69 on bb0128a, prior to the latest plugin and splash screen adjustments.
  • Time range observed via KEREDIT commits: 10:16 – 20:25.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 407h53+.

Brief conclusion

The day began with a visible regression in the editor: Google Photos did not clearly tell the client what to do when its authorisation had expired. It ended much further down the line: WooCommerce can now display a product listing driven by KEREDIT, without letting Woo invent a quantity, format or ‘Add to basket’ button alongside the creation workflow.

The guiding principle is simple: KEREDIT remains the industry standard, WooCommerce becomes the commercial gateway, and the printer must be able to configure this integration without having to decipher cryptic fields.

Google Photos: breaking the loop

The first symptom was on the publisher’s side: the Google Photos import would return with a ‘401’ on /api/google-photos/picker-sessions, then the interface would display a status that was too vague. The customer would mainly see ‘Try again’, click it, and end up back in the same loop.

The fix distinguished between two scenarios:

  • the KEREDIT session may still be valid;
  • the Google Photos link, however, may have expired, been revoked or be invalid.

The button has therefore become more explicit: the user must reconnect Google Photos. The workflow discards the old Google link, re-initiates OAuth and avoids giving the impression that a simple network retry can fix an invalid external authorisation.

Reference commit: 805fbf0 (fix: make Google Photos reconnect explicit).

Page previews: bringing reality back into view

Second visible fix: page previews should no longer remain as placeholders when the actual images are available. The page browser and overview now use more reliable preview areas, with asset URLs resolved, dedicated tests and expanded footer controls to prevent buttons from being too close together.

It’s not spectacular, but it’s exactly the sort of detail that builds trust in the editor: if a page exists, the interface must show that page, not an empty square that makes you doubt whether it’s been saved.

Reference commits:

  • 5008672 (fix: show real page previews by default) ;
  • 5ad4acb (fix: widen bottom preview controls).

WooCommerce: no longer buying before creating

The main task of the afternoon was the WooCommerce product page when a product is managed by KEREDIT.

Previously, WooCommerce still displayed its native controls: WooCommerce quantity, ‘Add to basket’ button, standard e-commerce logic. For a KEREDIT product, this is risky: the customer must not purchase a generic item before going through the editor and creating a customised project.

The connector now replaces this block with the expected workflow:

  • the direct WooCommerce controls are removed for KEREDIT products;
  • the creation button becomes the main action;
  • the quantity displayed is taken from the values authorised by KEREDIT;
  • launching the editor carries over the quantity, format and selected options.

Reference commit: 788557e (Fix KEREDIT Woo product purchase controls).

KEREDIT remains the master reference

Today’s key decision: WooCommerce must not invent product attributes. Quantities, formats and options come from KEREDIT. WooCommerce can choose what it displays to the customer, in what order, with what labelling and what tooltips, but it does not become the business data source.

The backend therefore exposes a product configuration that is readable by Woo. The plugin synchronises this data with the product page, keeps track of the last synchronisation, and provides a “Synchronise now” button to quickly push through any changes made in KEREDIT.

What is now covered:

  • permitted quantities;
  • available formats;
  • options from the KEREDIT product, for example paper or Accurio;
  • customisable customer labels;
  • visible customer descriptions;
  • visibility by attribute;
  • display order on the product details page.

Reference commit: bb0128a (Add KEREDIT Woo product options UI).

The admin UX was iterated live

The first version worked, but it was constrained by the WooCommerce “Product Data” panel: fields were too small, checkboxes were hard to read, accordions were poorly suited, and space was truncated. It was functional, but not acceptable for a printer who has to configure products all day long.

The KEREDIT configuration was therefore moved to a dedicated metabox, with a clearer structure:

  • a configuration header;
  • a synchronisation status;
  • an ‘Instant Sync’ button;
  • three tabs: login, customer view, advanced;
  • clear toggle switches;
  • full-width fields;
  • a client description by attribute;
  • an explicit display order;
  • an ‘Advanced’ mode reserved for technical constraints.

The client profile followed the same logic: the attributes are stacked, not aligned in a row, and then right-aligned to match the layout of the Woo theme observed.

Plugin versions released during this phase:

  • 0.1.29 : removal of native Woo controls and the KEREDIT Creation block;
  • 0.1.30 : manual synchronisation and initial KEREDIT attributes;
  • 0.1.31 : more user-friendly tabs, toggles and fields;
  • 0.1.32 : dedicated metabox outside the restrictive Woo panel;
  • 0.1.33 : stacked attributes and display order;
  • 0.1.34 : right-alignment of attributes on the product page.

Key commits:

  • ce15bda (Improve KEREDIT product admin UI) ;
  • bf5f3fa (Move KEREDIT product UI to metabox) ;
  • 342c242 (Stack KEREDIT product options) ;
  • 16bddf4 (Right align KEREDIT product attributes) ;
  • 34ae894 (Merge KEREDIT Woo product options UI).

Final polish: Amiga-style editor interface

The day ended with a deliberately stylised loading screen, in the style of Amiga Workbench: pixel art, an animated grid, a solid panel with sharp shadows, cyan/magenta/yellow/black, a workshop sheet, cutting marks, a ruler, a craft knife, a magnifying glass and loading indicators in discrete steps. This isn’t just a simple spinner placed in the middle of the page: it’s a buffer between WooCommerce and the editor.

The behaviour is also technically well-defined. The splash screen is handled by a dedicated store, cached in sessionStorage during launch, visible for at least two seconds to prevent overly rapid flashing, then animated out of view once the editor is ready. After 8.5 seconds, it switches to a long-wait state and offers to reload. If the launch fails, it displays an error message rather than leaving the customer facing a blank screen.

The work also addresses accessibility and validation: the overlay at role="status" reports its status via aria-live, complies with prefers-reduced-motion, and the Playwright smoke test now waits for the splash screen to appear and then disappear before validating the editor shell.

Reference commit: e64994f (feat: add editor launch splash).

What’s stable tonight

  • dev is aligned with origin/dev at e64994f.
  • The application versions are aligned at 0.6.70.
  • The KEREDIT WordPress connector is available at 0.1.34.
  • The WooCommerce product feed no longer offers direct purchase for a KEREDIT product.
  • The attributes displayed on the client side come from KEREDIT, but remain configurable within WooCommerce for order, labelling and visibility.
  • Reconnecting to Google Photos is now an explicit action.
  • Page previews now have a more concrete representation.
  • Launching the editor now features a proper loading screen, consistent with KEREDIT’s visual identity.

What remains to be monitored

The project has moved from a technical integration to a fully-fledged product interface. We will now need to test with products that are more complex than the test postcard: different paper types, different formats, workshop options, Accurio specifications, and customer descriptions that are short enough to remain legible on mobile devices.

The main point of focus is no longer “does Woo call KEREDIT?”. Rather, it is: can a printer configure ten different products without getting lost, and does a customer still understand what they are choosing before opening the editor?

This evening, the answer began to take shape.

description.source: Google Photos has been properly reconnected, page previews have been restored, and the WooCommerce plugin has been redesigned to allow KEREDIT to control quantities, formats and options.

title.source: Day 76 – WooCommerce becomes a genuine KEREDIT gateway

items.title: Day 76 – WooCommerce becomes a genuine KEREDIT gateway

body.source:
Session timetables

  • Tool used: Codex for analysis, correction and logging
  • Environments observed: Krampouz/KEREDIT at dépôt local krampouz, GOF at dépôt local gof, KEREDIT VPS [nom privé]
  • Date: Friday 5 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch: dev, clean and aligned with origin/dev
  • KEREDIT version at the end of the day: 0.6.66
  • End-of-day KEREDIT SHA: 9b261a1
  • VPS SHA verified after deployment: 9b261a19f1db950d81d292eba66bbba7b464a178
  • GOF branch: dev, aligned with origin/dev
  • Observed GOF SHA: b72a19f
  • Time range observed across KEREDIT commits: 09:26 -> 18:49
  • Amplitude observed via GOF commits: 09:26 -> 18:28
  • VPS backup created during deployment: /opt/[chemin privé]
  • Main KEREDIT commits:
    • 1545705 - Automate GOF dispatch from completed orders
    • eb0c929 - Notify Keredit immediately for Woo orders
    • 9dacb52 - chore: prepare GHCR beta deploy pipeline
    • bdea655 - chore: publish dev images from CI
    • dcb52d1 - fix: normalize proxy health host during deploy
    • c2c22d9 - Add builder clipart upload shortcut
    • e9fa741 - Support Accurio imposed quantity mappings
    • 15d003c - Harden business data deploy safety
    • 6f1304e - Refresh page overview asset URLs
    • f4dd2bf - Allow catalog decoration asset URLs
    • 1162f44 - Document cleanup audit and remove dead toolbar code
    • 9b261a1 - fix: refresh signed asset URLs in editor
  • Main GOF commits:
    • e61a930 - Add automatic Accurio submission toggle
    • b73afac - Fix GOF PDF asset and font rendering
    • f55efb2 - Sync KEREDIT Google fonts into GOF
    • e7b91d0 - Allow GOF dashboard to sync local fonts
    • 7b99d01 - Show print validation blockers in dashboard
    • fc156f0 - Allow operator override for print warnings
    • 44dc9d9 - Convert imposed quantities for Accurio orders
    • 3e2e126 - Pass Accurio runtime to GOF worker
    • b72a19f - Harden Accurio auto-submit readiness There are days when we code. Today, we mainly connected machines to one another. KEREDIT, GOF, Accurio and WooCommerce are no longer just names in an architecture. They’re starting to become a real journey, with orders, PDFs, fonts, quantities, validations, public URLs, containers, secrets, webhooks and production incidents. That’s probably why the day leaves you with a headache. It doesn’t feel like an isolated project. It feels like a workshop that comes to life bit by bit.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approx. 397h44+

Today’s feed

The thread remains the same as the one that appeared yesterday:

WooCommerce -> KEREDIT -> GOF -> Accurio Flux -> atelier

But today, this thread has started to carry some weight.

KEREDIT has learnt to automatically push data to GOF from completed orders. GOF has learnt to render assets and fonts more effectively, to synchronise KEREDIT’s Google Fonts, to display validation errors, to allow an operator to override certain warnings, and then to prepare for automatic submission to Accurio.

Accurio is no longer just a ‘future connector’. It is beginning to impose its exact constraints:

  • mandatory quantities;
  • available runtime in the GOF worker;
  • readiness prior to auto-submit;
  • distinction between operator warnings and hard blocks;
  • PDFs and assets accessible from the correct location;
  • fonts consistent with what KEREDIT sold to the client.

So the day didn’t just add features. It turned intentions into operational realities.

KEREDIT is pushing towards GOF

The first milestone on the KEREDIT side is clear: 1545705 automates GOF dispatch from completed orders.

This is a significant change, because it moves GOF from being a “tool that can be called” to being a “natural part of the order workflow”.

The commit adds:

  • an automatic dispatch option in the GOF configuration;
  • an associated Prisma field;
  • the PDF worker-side call;
  • worker tests;
  • a section in the PDF back office.

In short: when the order reaches the correct status, KEREDIT can prepare the GOF stage without waiting for any further manual intervention.

This is not yet a promise of zero supervision. It’s better than that: it’s a promise of a ‘workshop-first’ approach. The system proceeds automatically whenever possible, but the checkpoints remain visible.

GOF is learning to operate like KEREDIT

On the GOF side, it’s been a very busy day.

The commit b73afac fixes the PDF rendering of assets and fonts. This isn’t just a cosmetic change. If GOF is to become the PDF engine, it must reproduce exactly what the publisher displayed, not produce a vaguely similar interpretation.

The commit f55efb2 then adds synchronisation of KEREDIT’s Google Fonts within GOF. This is exactly the sort of detail that reveals the true contract:

  • the client selects a font from KEREDIT;
  • KEREDIT persists this choice;
  • GOF must be able to resolve it locally;
  • the PDF must remain consistent;
  • Accurio must not discover a font substitution at the last minute.

The GOF dashboard has also become more sophisticated:

  • details of rendering events;
  • print validation blocks;
  • progress whilst a job is open;
  • selection and deletion of jobs;
  • a better-integrated jobs panel;
  • a cleaner sidebar.

GOF is becoming less of a hidden API and more of a proper operator console.

Accurio is establishing its own terminology

Today’s work on Accurio was very practical.

The GOF commit 44dc9d9 converts the imposition quantities for Accurio orders. On the KEREDIT side, e9fa741 adds the corresponding mappings to the exports and the admin panel.

This is an important point: printer quantities are not always the same as gross commercial quantities. The print shop sells an order, but production may be subject to imposition, batch, sheet or service logic.

The system has now therefore started to account for this difference rather than hiding it.

The latest GOF commits (3e2e126, b72a19f) also enhance Accurio readiness. Auto-submit must not be a dangerous toggle. The runtime must be available in the worker, and the minimum conditions must be met before anything is sent.

This is the right approach: automate, yes; send blindly, no.

Deployment is also becoming a product development focus

KEREDIT has also made progress on the deployment pipeline.

The morning commits pave the way for GHCR:

  • modernised GitHub Actions runtime;
  • beta deployment pipeline set up;
  • dev images published from CI;
  • workflow token for GHCR pull requests;
  • normalised proxy host health.

15d003c then adds a more robust safeguard: the security of business data during deployment.

The deployment script now takes a snapshot of the business data before and after, and rejects any unexpected changes unless there is explicit opt-in. This is exactly the sort of protection that matters when you start handling orders, products, mappings and production flows.

Deployment is no longer just about “restarting containers”. It becomes a contract of trust.

A fire in production: the photos disappear

The end of the day was a bit of a fire-fighting session.

In the live editor, the photos were no longer appearing. The console was displaying a continuous loop of ‘403’ messages:

/api/assets/public/.../thumbnail
/api/assets/public/.../preview
/api/assets/public/.../original

The diagnosis was quite clear: the signed URLs for the assets had expired, but the Photos panel was holding onto the old URLs for too long. It wasn’t a missing image, nor a grid rendering issue. It was a lifecycle contract.

The fix 9b261a1 adds a front-end helper that reads the expires from the URLs /api/assets/public/..., then schedules a silent refresh before they expire. It also refreshes when focus is regained if the URLs are already too close to expiry.

The version was updated from 0.6.65 to 0.6.66, then urgently deployed to the VPS via the manual path from local to VPS.

Post-deployment verification:

  • .deploy-sha VPS: 9b261a19f1db950d81d292eba66bbba7b464a178;
  • VPS packages: 0.6.66;
  • Public API health OK;
  • Public frontend OK;
  • Public bundle served via 0.6.66;
  • script smoke checks OK.

Important point: the fix is narrow in scope. It does not arbitrarily extend the lifetime of signed URLs. It adheres to the security model and corrects the client-side refresh.

Addendum – The fixes that followed

The first fix for photos resolved the issue of images disappearing in the editor, but live testing immediately revealed a second, more subtle problem: the Google Photos import.

In the console, the following call returned an error:

/api/google-photos/picker-sessions -> 401

At first glance, this looked like a lost KEREDIT session. In reality, the VPS logs told a different story: immediately after this `401`, `/api/auth/me` responded with `200`. The client was therefore still connected to KEREDIT.

The problem lay in our error handling logic: when Google Photos could no longer be reconnected properly, or when the Google token had expired or been revoked, the route /picker-sessions would return 401. This status triggered both a mental and technical misdiagnosis. We assumed there was an invalid KEREDIT session, whereas the real issue was the Google Photos connection.

The commit 7dda00c corrected this behaviour:

  • the KEREDIT session remains distinct from the Google login;
  • an expired or rejected Google Photos token now returns `409`;
  • the message is now actionable: Google Photos must be reconnected;
  • this scenario is covered by an integration test.

Then, one final UX pitfall emerged. The modal displayed the message correctly, but it only offered Réessayer. For a user, this creates an absurd loop: they click, the Picker call restarts, Google Photos responds again with 409, and nothing progresses.

The commit 805fbf0 therefore changed the screen:

  • in the event of 409, the modal displays a main ‘Reconnect Google Photos’ button;
  • this button clears the old Google link on the KEREDIT side;
  • it opens the Google OAuth flow directly;
  • the customer no longer needs to realise that they first had to click ‘Déconnecter’, return to the previous screen, and then reconnect.

These two fixes have been deployed to the VPS as a hotfix in the same version as 0.6.66.

The final SHA verified following these changes is:

805fbf0edd4f54d70de0fef80504a85a861c842a

In between, the f365618 commit also closed a number of clean-up follow-ups: documented structural debt, completed clean-up audit, PDF/email/script adjustments, and updated tracking documentation. This wasn’t the most visible work from the client’s perspective, but it forms part of the same effort: keeping the project readable whilst production demands rapid fixes.

Cleaning up whilst things are heating up

The day wasn’t all about workflows and incidents.

1162f44 It also involved a comprehensive clean-up review and the removal of dead code from the toolbar. It’s easy to underestimate this on a day like this, but it’s important.

When GOF, Accurio, WooCommerce, webhooks and deployment are all changing at the same time, there’s a risk of letting dead code accumulate. The audit and documentation clean-up kept the map clear:

  • BIBLIOTHEQUE.md ;
  • CHANGELOG.md ;
  • README.md ;
  • docs/HOME.md ;
  • docs/audits/2026-06-05-revue-globale-nettoyage.md ;
  • plugin guides and front-end debugging;
  • theme standardisation audit.

It’s not spectacular, but it’s what stops you from losing the thread when production starts pulling on all the strings.

What’s holding up tonight

Tonight, several things are holding up better than yesterday.

KEREDIT can now automatically push to GOF from completed jobs. GOF renders assets and fonts better. KEREDIT fonts can be synchronised in GOF. Print warnings are now visible and can be managed by an operator. Accurio receives a model that better aligns with its constraints, particularly regarding imposed quantities. The deployment is better protected against unexpected changes to business data.

And above all, the KEREDIT VPS has weathered a genuine production incident with a quick fix that was tested and deployed properly.

The system is not trouble-free, but it is more robust.

What remains fragile

Vulnerability remains throughout the entire workflow.

We now have many components capable of functioning:

  • WooCommerce can notify KEREDIT;
  • KEREDIT can maintain context and dispatch;
  • GOF can render, validate and prepare Accurio;
  • Accurio can receive a structured command;
  • the VPS can be redeployed with safeguards in place.

However, a workflow is only validated if it runs end-to-end with a real order and a deliberately simple product.

Areas to monitor:

  • exact consistency between the KEREDIT sales quantity and the quantity set in Accurio;
  • public or LAN availability of PDFs from Accurio’s perspective;
  • effective font resolution on the GOF machine;
  • distinction between a ‘forceable warning’ and a ‘hard block’;
  • status of the GOF job after auto-submit;
  • behaviour of the editor after long open sessions, now that the signed URLs have been refreshed.

To be continued tomorrow

Tomorrow, don’t try to replay everything.

A good replay is short:

un produit postcard
-> une commande Woo
-> un projet KEREDIT
-> un dispatch GOF
-> un rendu PDF contrôle
-> une validation opérateur
-> un envoi Accurio

Focus on a single scenario, a single product, a single order, and note every point where it breaks.

It’s been a tough day because it affected the entire chain. But that’s also what makes it worthwhile: KEREDIT is no longer just a web-to-print editor. It’s starting to become a workshop system linked to production.
