title.source: Day 75 – From GOF to Accurio, then a fire in production

items.title: Day 75 – From GOF to Accurio, then a fire in production

body.source:
Session timetables

  • Tool used: Codex for analysis and logging support
  • Environments monitored: Krampouz/KEREDIT local in dépôt local krampouz and GOF in dépôt local gof
  • Date: Thursday 4 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch: dev, clean, aligned with origin/dev
  • KEREDIT version observed: 0.6.61
  • KEREDIT SHA observed at the end of the day: 4508cf6
  • GOF branch: dev, clean, aligned with origin/dev
  • GOF SHA observed at the end of the day: 9d5fdc9
  • Amplitude observed by KEREDIT commits: 11:32 -> 20:06
  • Time span observed via GOF commits: 11:26 -> 19:09
  • Estimated active time: a busy day with multiple repositories; not measured precisely
  • Main KEREDIT commits:
    • 401c22c - Extend GOF export contract for Accurio
    • 609758c - Add GOF Flux integration settings
    • 09b75b5 - Add GOF pairing flow
    • ad86abf - Add GOF Flux client setup help
    • cc77fe0 - Clarify GOF connection status
    • cf39c37 - Document GOF Flux client connection
    • 22f28fc - Read Accurio catalog through GOF
    • 6005f41 - Clarify Accurio catalog is read through GOF
    • 03d44bd - Prefer Woo customer context for GOF exports
    • 78a0929 - Reuse Woo cart lock for editor cart updates
    • 861c13d - Automate WooCommerce webhook setup
    • 4508cf6 - Allow Woo checkout repair from admin
  • Main GOF commits:
    • 729c4ba - Add Accurio production connector
    • 2a160d8 - Add GOF client configuration UI
    • 7e796a5 - docs: add GOF architecture memo
    • 87cb2e5 - Replace GOF browser auth prompt with session login
    • 0185c78 - Add GOF configuration help panel
    • 7abe5fd - Simplify KEREDIT synchronization setup
    • e880de2 - Clarify KEREDIT connection flow
    • bb033fc - Update KEREDIT connection documentation
    • c84345c - Apply JetBrains Mono to GOF backoffice
    • e2c03ad - Tokenize GOF backoffice theme
    • b4d6e8f - Delete GOF API tokens permanently
    • 5010807 - Simplify GOF Accurio configuration
    • a597a7a - Expose complete Accurio catalog from GOF
    • 025b66d - Return client errors for GOF API validation failures
    • 9d5fdc9 - Format Accurio jobs with order and sender fields There are days when the project moves forward in a straight line. And then there’s this one. KEREDIT, GOF, Accurio, WooCommerce, the back office, the development machine, live tests, error messages, tokens, public and LAN URLs: everything ended up on the table at the same time. So the feeling of being a bit lost is no accident. It reflects what happened technically: the product has moved beyond the simple setup and is now starting to touch the real production pipeline. What’s impressive is that this scattered nature has a pattern. It tells the same story, seen from several different angles.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 388h21+

The actual flow emerges

The crux of the day can be summed up in a single line:

WooCommerce -> KEREDIT -> GOF -> Accurio Flux -> atelier

Up to this point, each segment already had substance.

KEREDIT was able to receive a project, maintain client context, expose a back-office system, and send a job to a PDF renderer. GOF was able to act as the local renderer, generate artefacts, and keep a production log. Accurio was the industrial ecosystem we needed to integrate with, with its API, catalogue, printers, services and network constraints.

Today, the task has been to pass real data across these boundaries.

This isn’t just a minor UI tweak. It’s a fundamental shift: we’re no longer just testing an editor; we’re testing a production line.

Accurio is part of the contract

The first KEREDIT project of the day extended the GOF export payload for Accurio.

The payload no longer simply states “here is a project to be delivered”. It now carries the expected production details:

  • client context;
  • order context;
  • Accurio product name;
  • target printer;
  • order prefix;
  • delivery type;
  • Accurio services selected from the KEREDIT options.

On the GOF side, the commit 729c4ba added the Accurio production connector. The workflow in GOF establishes an important rule: Accurio receives a document POST /api/createOrder that is already compliant. For this workflow, no Accurio transformation script should become the central workaround.

This is precisely the right approach to accountability:

  • KEREDIT remains the business authority: customer, order, product sold, options, mapping.
  • GOF prepares the PDF, keeps it available and submits the order.
  • Accurio manages production and printing.

The difficulty arises when words need to be translated into precise terms: Accurio product, Accurio printer, Accurio services, PDF URL accessible from the Accurio server.

GOF becomes configurable

GOF has evolved significantly today.

The forge is no longer just a local app with a PDF pipeline. It now features a usable configuration interface:

  • Accurio connector;
  • client configuration UI;
  • session-based back-office login instead of plain browser authentication;
  • built-in configuration help;
  • customer documentation;
  • simplification of the KEREDIT synchronisation process;
  • clean removal of old automatic API tokens;
  • full reading of the Accurio catalogue from GOF;
  • API errors returned in a readable format.

The GOF documentation produced today also sends an important signal:

  • docs/flux-keredit-gof-accurio.md sets out the technical specifications;
  • docs/procedure-client-configuration-keredit-gof-accurio.md provides a non-technical customer procedure;
  • docs/architecture-gof-memo-2026-06-04.html and .pdf set out the architectural intent;
  • docs/operations-gof.md whilst docs/backoffice-gof.md handle the operational side.

GOF therefore assumes its role as a workshop: not a hidden library, but a configured, visible, testable local machine, with an operator at the centre.

KEREDIT is learning to connect to GOF

On the KEREDIT side, the back-office GOF Flux has become much more tangible.

Two migrations have been added:

  • 20260604113000_add_gof_integration_config ;
  • 20260604124500_add_gof_pairing_code.

These allow the GOF configuration to be stored, followed by a temporary login code. The principle is simple for the client:

  1. KEREDIT generates a login code.
  2. GOF receives this code on its configuration screen.
  3. GOF creates a technical token.
  4. GOF sends this token to KEREDIT.
  5. KEREDIT stores it in encrypted form and tests the connection.

This is much better than a field saying “paste a secret token somewhere”, because the customer’s action becomes clear: connecting two tools, not handling a technical key.

The KEREDIT back office also displays the connection status, GOF tests and the Accurio catalogue read status more clearly.

A policy issue was rectified this afternoon: KEREDIT must not read the Accurio catalogue directly. The Accurio catalogue is read by GOF, because GOF is installed in the workshop and can connect to the Accurio Flux server. KEREDIT then utilises this data via GOF.

This detail may seem minor, but it prevents an unstable architecture. Accurio belongs to the workshop network, not the KEREDIT VPS.

WooCommerce closes the loop

By the end of the day, WooCommerce had been brought back into the loop.

This isn’t a separate issue. The GOF/Accurio workflow requires both the order context and the customer context. Without these, the production team receives a PDF, but not enough business logic to process it.

The end-of-day commits therefore dealt with:

  • the preferred Woo customer context for GOF exports;
  • reusing the WooCommerce cart lock for updates from the editor;
  • the automation of the WooCommerce webhook configuration;
  • checkout repair via the admin panel.

We can see the same logic here as with GOF: real-world testing reveals hidden contracts. An editor project does not exist in isolation. It must remain consistent with the shopping basket, the order, the webhooks and the client identity.

Bugs aren’t just noise

The quote of the day could be: “I’m uncovering issues everywhere whilst testing”.

Yes. And that’s probably a good sign, even if it’s tiring.

Problems crop up everywhere because testing now crosses the system’s boundaries:

  • browser/back-office boundary;
  • the KEREDIT/GOF boundary;
  • the VPS/development machine boundary;
  • public URL / LAN URL boundary;
  • readable token / encrypted technical token boundary;
  • Accurio catalogue / KEREDIT product mapping boundary;
  • publisher project / WooCommerce order boundary;
  • boundary between generated PDF and printable order.

As long as each component was tested in isolation, these issues remained hidden. Live testing brings them to light. This is not a single regression with a simple cause. It is the gradual discovery of the true production contract.

The correct response, therefore, is not to reopen everything. It is to turn every surprise into a contract:

  • who is the authority for this data?
  • Who is authorised to call which service?
  • Which URL must be accessible from which machine?
  • Which status should be visible to the customer or the operator?
  • Which error should halt the flow rather than giving the impression that everything is fine?

What’s already in place

Tonight, there are some solid foundations.

KEREDIT and GOF are both on dev, clean, up to date, with a consistent commit history. The KEREDIT versions have been realigned to 0.6.61. The back office now has a proper start to its interface at GOF Flux. Code pairing provides a more robust customer experience. GOF reads Accurio from the correct location. Client and operator documentation is in place. WooCommerce continues to move closer to the production environment.

Most importantly: the architecture has retained the correct distribution.

KEREDIT is not becoming a remote Accurio machine. GOF does not read KEREDIT’s internal tables as the primary contract. Accurio is not becoming the place where KEREDIT data is corrected. Each tool is starting to find its place.

What remains fragile

The vulnerability does not yet lie in a single file. It lies in the entire workflow.

We still need to calmly test a minimal workflow:

  1. Check that the KEREDIT VPS is indeed serving the expected SHA before any live testing.
  2. Open GOF and validate its Accurio configuration.
  3. From the Accurio server, check that the GOF URL for the PDFs is accessible.
  4. Connect KEREDIT to GOF using a temporary code.
  5. Test GOF from KEREDIT.
  6. Read the Accurio catalogue via GOF.
  7. Map a single KEREDIT product to a single Accurio product.
  8. Send a known project to GOF.
  9. Check the PDF in GOF.
  10. Send to Accurio.
  11. Note down each error along with its exact boundaries.

This walkthrough must remain concise. One product, one order, one PDF, one printer. Not the whole shop, not all formats, not all business scenarios.

What this tells us about the beta

The postcard beta is no longer just about a nice-looking, stable editor.

It’s becoming a matter of workshop trust:

  • can the customer place an order?
  • Does KEREDIT retain the correct context?
  • Does GOF produce a controllable artefact?
  • Does Accurio receive a usable job?
  • Does the operator know where to look when something breaks?

It was an impressive day because it brought this level of detail to light.

There are still lots of moving parts, but they’re starting to form a chain. It’s not comfortable, but it’s more realistic than reassuring. And for a workshop-first project, this is probably the right step.

Back to work tomorrow

Tomorrow, don’t try to ‘test everything’.

Aim to test a single story from start to finish:

un produit postcard -> une commande Woo -> un projet KEREDIT -> un job GOF -> un PDF contrôle -> un envoi Accurio

If this story works, even with some tweaks, today’s work will take on a new significance: it will no longer be an overwhelming jumble, but the moment when the pieces began to come together as a flow.

description.source: A busy day of integration between KEREDIT, GOF, Accurio Flux and WooCommerce: guided configuration, pairing, the Accurio catalogue read by GOF, production contracts and bugs identified during live testing.

title.source: Day 74 – KEREDIT, GOF, Accurio: the flow leaves the workshop

items.title: Day 74 – KEREDIT, GOF, Accurio: the flow leaves the workshop

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Software used: Codex
  • Environments observed: Krampouz/KEREDIT local in dépôt local krampouz, GOF in dépôt local gof, quick check of dépôt local keredit-site
  • Date: Wednesday 3 June 2026
  • KEREDIT/Krampouz branch observed: dev
  • GOF branch observed: dev
  • keredit-site repository: no Git commits dated 3 June 2026 on main or via --all
  • Time range observed by KEREDIT/Krampouz commits: 08:35 -> 18:44
  • Amplitude observed via GOF commits: 08:34 -> 19:27
  • Estimated active time: a long, split day, not measured precisely
  • Main KEREDIT/Krampouz commits:
    • 6ed046c - fix upload diagnostics and bug report capture
    • 1d4f0e0 - fix asset preview refresh after upload
    • 652b68a - fix photo upload preview key creation
    • 40bbab6 - fix asset pipeline contracts and thumbnails
    • f1a25b6 - polish editor save icon
    • b97124c - fix autosave drag freezes
    • 6548090 - fix text style controls
    • 7e12d3e - update photo frame fit icon
    • ddabd28 - polish launch loading and users query
    • 341540f - fix circular launch logo
    • 1e71664 - chore(dev): adapter le runtime local au Mac
  • Main GOF commits:
    • ccfb2d6 - Initial GOF forge baseline
    • 8f9dcc8 - Ignore local backups and Playwright artifacts
    • 621f1a1 - Document client reverse proxy setup
    • 3c6c49c - feat: show job details in fullscreen modal The 3 June post was missing, but the day itself is clearly documented. It’s actually quite clear: KEREDIT spent the day ironing out beta bugs relating to assets, uploads, autosave and the editor’s visible controls, whilst GOF finally became a proper Git repository with a working PDF workshop. It’s not quite the big Accurio build of 4 June yet. It’s the useful run-up: the moment when the editor stops faltering on simple tasks, and when the build environment ceases to be merely a working folder.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 379h41+

KEREDIT: making the beta less fragile

The first KEREDIT focus of the day is direct uploads and diagnostics.

The commit 6ed046c added an R2 probe script, two reference CORS configurations, deployment notes and a more explicit upload specification. The bug report button has also been streamlined to better capture what matters rather than generating noise.

It’s a subtle but crucial issue for the beta: if a client or tester uploads a photo and the asset doesn’t appear, we need to know whether the problem lies with the browser, R2, the backend, the frontend poll, the worker or the thumbnail. Without diagnostics, every test looks like a system-wide failure.

Assets: quickly see what you’ve just imported

The rest of the day revolved around the asset contract.

The commits 1d4f0e0, 652b68a and, most importantly, 40bbab6 have tightened up several layers:

  • refreshing the preview after upload;
  • creation of a preview key for imported photos;
  • asset contract backend helpers;
  • audit and repair scripts;
  • backend tests for the asset contract;
  • corrections to the pipeline worker;
  • front-end formatting of assets;
  • thumbnails in the options panels;
  • consistency between upload status, preview and editor display.

The key point is this: for the beta, ‘uploaded’ and ‘preview_ready’ are the statuses that must instil confidence in the user. ‘print_ready’ remains a production concern, but it must not block visibility in the editor.

This day has therefore refocused attention on the right thing: the user must be able to see their image, understand that it is available, and continue editing without having to wait for the entire production pipeline to have finished processing.

Save, autosave and visible action

Commit f1a25b6 completed the move of the save button to the global header.

This detail had already been refined through screenshots: size, line style, legibility, and ensuring there were no duplicates in the toolbar. This isn’t just cosmetic. For a client-side editor, the save button must be where the eye naturally looks for it, and it must not compete with style controls.

The commit b97124c addressed a more fundamental issue: autosave freezes during dragging.

The Postcard beta needs basic gestures to remain fluid. Moving a photo, text or decorative element must not give the impression that the application has frozen because it is persisting too aggressively at the wrong moment. The fix is a step in the right direction: less friction during interaction, with persistence at the right pace.

Text and editing controls

The commit 6548090 has fixed the text style controls.

It added common components for colour swatches and font selection, dedicated helpers for text styles, and tests for the font catalogue and controls. The text panel and toolbar have been realigned.

This issue is important because, whilst text is not the main area to be reopened before the beta, it must remain stable. A text tool that loses its font, displays colours incorrectly, or shows inconsistencies between the panel and the toolbar immediately gives the impression of an unfinished editor.

So today’s work didn’t mark the relaunch of a typographic ambition. Instead, it consolidated what already exists to ensure that the controls already on display remain consistent.

Woo launch and round logo

The late afternoon also saw fixes to visible details relating to the Woo launch and the logo.

The commits ddabd28 and 341540f refined the splash screen, the admin user query and the round logo on the splash page. The commit 7e12d3e adjusted the fit icon for the photo frame.

The approach remains the same as in previous days: minor visual inconsistencies are not mere details when preparing for a closed beta. They are indicators. KEREDIT must give the impression of a polished tool, even if the entire production workflow is not yet finalised.

Local runtime: adapting the workstation

The final KEREDIT commit of the day, 1e71664, adapted the local runtime for Mac.

It affected the dev scripts, the local DB bootstrap, the backend reset, the status, the start/stop commands and the workstation recovery guides. A helper scripts/dev-runtime-lib.sh was added to centralise part of this logic.

This is less product-related, but very important for the future: a beta cannot be properly prepared if the development workstation misrepresents its purpose. So 3 June was also a day spent making the environment more reliable.

GOF: a clean start for the forge

On the GOF front, 3 June is even more straightforward.

At 08:34, the commit ‘ccfb2d6’ established the initial baseline for the build system: Node app, Dockerfile, Docker Compose, Postgres, Redis, worker, dashboard, storage, queue, PDF renderer, installation scripts and operational documentation.

The GOF folder thus ceased to be merely a collection of notes. It became a repository.

The main components are:

  • an app gof-forge-app;
  • a rendering worker;
  • a BullMQ queue;
  • a Postgres database;
  • local storage and R2;
  • a basic low-level PDF renderer using pdf-lib and sharp;
  • an operator dashboard;
  • documentation on installation, security, HTTPS exposure and operations;
  • a synchronisation script to the workshop machine.

The commit `8f9dcc8` then cleans up the repository by ignoring local backups and Playwright artefacts. This is a clean-up commit, but it’s important: a workshop forge must not begin its Git life with local backups as a source of noise.

Client-side reverse proxy and workshop exposure

The commit 621f1a1 documents the client-side reverse proxy installation.

It adds docs/reverse-proxy-installation-client.md and connects README.md, docs/exposition-https-autonome.md and the Ubuntu runbook. This is already a real-world issue: GOF must reside within the workshop, but certain services must be properly accessible from the outside or from KEREDIT, depending on the traffic flows.

This isn’t yet the pairing session scheduled for 4 June. It’s preparation for the demonstration: how to make the forge accessible without turning every client into a system administrator.

GOF back office: view jobs

The commit 3c6c49c, made at the end of the day, adds a full-screen modal for displaying job details.

It modifies `app/src/server.js`, updates the dependencies and enhances the operations/runbook documentation. This is a strong product signal for GOF: the operator must not only know that a job exists, but must be able to open it, read its payload, its artefacts and its events in a user-friendly interface.

A PDF forge is not a black box. It must explain what it received, what it produced, and where it failed.

What 3 June tells us about 4 June

The post from 4 June describes the entire workflow:

WooCommerce -> KEREDIT -> GOF -> Accurio Flux -> atelier

The 3 June post, on the other hand, covers the preparation for this workflow.

KEREDIT works on user inputs: uploads, assets, autosave, text, launch, local runtime.

GOF is working on the production environment: Git repository, Docker stack, worker, renderer, dashboard, reverse proxy, operations.

The following day, these two worlds began to communicate more openly with one another regarding Accurio. But without 3 June, 4 June would have meant less. First, each side needed to be a bit more organised.

What’s holding up

By the end of the day, several things are more robust:

  • uploads have better diagnostics;
  • asset previews have a clearer specification;
  • thumbnails reappear more quickly in the interface;
  • autosave causes fewer issues with interactions;
  • text controls are better modularised and tested;
  • saving is handled in the global header;
  • the local runtime is better suited to the workstation;
  • GOF exists as a Git repository and as a Stack Atelier;
  • the GOF back office has started to provide visibility to operators.

The keredit-site repository, however, shows no Git activity on 3 June. The KEREDIT day visible in the logs is therefore driven by the Krampouz/KEREDIT monorepo, not by the separate showcase site or WordPress site.

What remains fragile

The main vulnerability remains the end-to-end workflow.

Each component has progressed, but the whole is not yet a beta workflow that can be smoothly replayed. Assets must remain visible without having to wait for production. Autosave must remain seamless during interaction. GOF must be accessible from the right locations, not just from the dev workstation. And the future Accurio link must not blur the division of responsibilities: KEREDIT for the project and the order, GOF for the forge and the operator, Accurio for production.

Resumption

The logical next steps after 3 June are straightforward:

  1. re-run a photo import and check that the preview becomes visible without having to wait for ‘print_ready’;
  2. test a long drag with autosave enabled;
  3. check the text controls displayed in the toolbar;
  4. confirm that the dev scripts correctly indicate that the runtime has loaded;
  5. open GOF, create or inspect a job, and check that the operator details are legible;
  6. prepare the KEREDIT → GOF bridge without making GOF an opaque dependency.

3 June wasn’t a spectacular day in terms of a single major deliverable. It was better than that: a day of fine-tuning. The publisher is becoming less anxious, the assets are becoming more predictable, and GOF has moved from the draft stage to the start of production.

description.source: A pivotal day marking the stabilisation of the KEREDIT beta, direct uploads, assets, autosave, text checks and the launch of GOF’s Git repository as a PDF workshop platform.

title.source: Day 73 – Stabilising the editor whilst GOF takes shape

items.title: Day 73 – Stabilising the editor whilst GOF takes shape

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: local Krampouz/KEREDIT repository, ‘dev’ branch, plus inspection of the GOF folder dépôt local gof
  • Date: Tuesday 2 June 2026
  • Branch: dev for Krampouz; GOF outside the Git repository active at the time of the review (git status failed in dépôt local gof)
  • Known application version: 0.6.49
  • Reference WordPress/WooCommerce plugin version: 0.1.27
  • Last SHA pushed at the end of the session: 9dc39ce
  • Time range covered by commits: 09:09 -> 19:20
  • GOF duration observed via mtimes: 08:19 -> 19:25 in dépôt local gof
  • Estimated active time: a day of intermittent work, not measured precisely
  • Main commits pushed:
    • 7f5469f - docs: add PDF generation analysis references
    • 95c8e70 - docs: add 2026-06-01 workshop pause journal
    • 45bbc89 - Add editable circular logo framing
    • 9dc39ce - Commit remaining beta updates 2 June was a real return to work after the lull on 1 June. Not a major product roll-out. Rather, a day of getting things back on track, with several issues clearly highlighting where KEREDIT stands ahead of the beta launch: the PDF documents, the log, the small customisation details visible to the printer, and tidying up the tests relating to the beta journey.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the log began: approximately 368h48+, not recalculated

PDF references

The morning began with the addition of documentation relating to PDF generation.

The repository now contains more robust references for analysing the future output:

  • addition of an HTML analysis in ;
  • addition of a GWG reference in docs/analyse/références/pdf-specs/;
  • alignment in BIBLIOTHEQUE.md and docs/HOME.md.

This isn’t yet the renderer project itself. It’s the preparation layer that prevents us from creating PDFs ‘by feel’.

The context remains the same: KEREDIT must produce a complete, versioned payload, and GOF must become the engine capable of transforming this payload into a production PDF. No default fallback to Puppeteer. No need for a massive screenshot when a single-page document will suffice.

Retrospective log for 1 June

The post dated 1 June was created retrospectively.

Its purpose was simple: to state that nothing had happened on the workshop front that day.

It’s less spectacular than a new feature, but it’s important for the project’s historical record. An undocumented ‘blank’ day quickly becomes a gap in the timeline. A documented ‘blank’ day becomes a piece of information: the beta plan was maintained, with no hidden agenda and no implicit approval.

Printer logo: the detail that catches the eye straight away

The main visible topic of the day was the printer logo.

The request seemed cosmetic: the logo had to be in a circle. In practice, the issue affected several areas:

  • back-office sidebar;
  • admin preview;
  • login;
  • password reset;
  • editor bar;
  • Personnalisation page;
  • export/import and persistence of the current theme.

The first version was too simplistic: it would sometimes display a square where an area was supposed to be round, or a circle that didn’t quite match the final framing. The problem eventually pointed to a more interesting cause: in KEREDIT, UI radii are deliberately locked to 0px, and rounded-full also depended on the token radiusFull.

Conclusion: in this specific case, the circle is not a generic style. It is a business-specific rendering constraint for the logo.

The final correction therefore added:

  • logoTransform in the parent theme (x, y, scale);
  • a centralised ‘BrandLogo’ that effectively masks the final circular rendering;
  • a cropping tool available after upload;
  • a common cropping canvas shared between the preview and the final render;
  • an explicit circular guide that no longer depends on radius tokens;
  • Playwright tests dedicated to the logo workflow.

The key point is consistency: what the admin sees within the cropping circle must be what subsequently appears in the final logo.

GOF: the forge moves beyond the draft stage

The first version of the post didn’t do enough justice to the GOF work. It was an editorial oversight: we’d specifically decided not to launch a second blog, and so to track the development of the PDF Atelier forge here, even when it exists outside the Krampouz folder.

Inspection carried out in:

dépôt local gof

Important point: this folder is not an active Git repository at the time of inspection. git status returned fatal: not à git repository. For this day, the GOF source of truth is therefore the contents of the files and their modification dates.

The mtimes provide a true snapshot of 2 June:

  • docs/moteur-pdf-bas-niveau.md modified at 08:19;
  • app/package.json, package-lock.json, config.js, pdf-renderer.js, queue.js, storage.js modified around 09:59–10:00;
  • .dockerignore, .env.example, app/Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml updated at around 10.05;
  • README.md, docs/backoffice-gof.md, docs/operations-gof.md, docs/runbook-installation-ubuntu.md amended at approximately 10.07;
  • app/src/job-service.js edited at 10.18;
  • app/src/db.js edited at 11.34;
  • scripts/sync-to-forge.sh edited at 19:17;
  • app/src/server.js edited at 19:25.

This is no longer just a statement of intent. GOF now has an application framework.

GOF technical framework

The GOF folder contains a Node app gof-forge-app written in CommonJS, with:

  • bullmq ioredis for the job queue;
  • pg and a Postgres database for tracking jobs;
  • pdf-lib sharp for initial native PDF rendering and image normalisation;
  • AWS S3 SDK to read R2 assets;
  • pdfjs-dist to view the generated PDFs in the dashboard.

The webdocker-compose.ymls a complete development stack:

  • Postgres 16;
  • Redis 7 with append-only;
  • GOF dashboard on 8080;
  • separate rendering worker;
  • Nginx Proxy Manager;
  • Dozzle in ops profile;
  • persistent volumes data/, fonts/ and NVMe storage spaces cache, work, tmp, output-staging.

The script scripts/sync-to-forge.sh prepares synchronisation to [compte]@[hôte]:/opt/[chemin privé], excluding .env, data/, node_modules, Playwright captures, backups and .git.

Backoffice Flux

docs/backoffice-gof.md documents a real workshop interface, served by app/src/server.js:

  • folders by status: received, queue, generation, success, failures, cancellations, validations;
  • sortable and searchable job table;
  • detail panel with JSON payload, reports, assets, artefacts, events and operator actions;
  • PDF.js viewer to open the local artefact;
  • operator actions: cancel, retry, approve for printing.

GOF routes exist on the application side:

  • POST /api/render-jobs to create a job;
  • GET /api/render-jobs to list;
  • GET /api/render-jobs/:id to view;
  • POST /api/render-jobs/:id/cancel ;
  • POST /api/render-jobs/:id/retry ;
  • POST /api/render-jobs/:id/approve ;
  • endpoints for signed asset URLs and reading local artefacts.

The database creates the following tablesrender_jobsrender_assetsrender_artifactsrender_events and operator_actions. This is exactly the right terminology for a forge: work, assets, artefacts, events and human actions.

PDF Renderer v1

The first renderer is located at app/src/pdf-renderer.js.

It does not launch Chromium. It creates a PDF using pdf-lib, converts the dimensions from mm to PDF points, sets MediaBox, BleedBox and TrimBox, and draws:

  • page backgrounds;
  • text as PDF text objects with Helvetica as the fallback font;
  • vector rectangles;
  • images and clipart rendered from assets[].storage_key via R2, then normalised using sharp.

The renderer also produces:

  • render-report.json ;
  • print-validation-report.json ;
  • an SHA-256 checksum for the PDF;
  • warnings for missing assets, fallback fonts, and vector SVGs not yet supported.

This is not yet the final pre-press engine, and the blog post must make that clear. But it is a first working build: a payload is input, a job is tracked, a master PDF is output, and a report explains what has been done.

PDF Doctrine

The GOF documentation also reinforces the approach:

  • docs/inspiration-dalim-twist-forge-pdf.md translates the DALIM/TWiST logic into a GOF pipeline: ingestion, pre-volumisation, normalisation, display list, native rendering, post-processing, final check;
  • docs/moteur-pdf-bas-niveau.md establishes the principle of a native PDF writer, without Puppeteer/Playwright/Chromium in the nominal pipeline;
  • docs/preparation-pdf.md is now marked as a historical draft, with an official note stating that the Puppeteer approaches are no longer the preferred direction;
  • docs/backoffice-gof.md links this doctrine to a concrete operational interface.

The underlying principle is sound: GOF is not ‘just another PDF exporter’. It is a production pipeline. KEREDIT retains control over the project, the order, the templates and the assets; GOF consumes a standalone PDF payload, produces artefacts and ensures its decisions are auditable.

GOF in the KEREDIT back office

The end-of-day commit also included the first elements of GOF exposure on the Krampouz admin side.

The added and modified files show the integration on the KEREDIT side:

  • backend/src/routes/admin/gof.ts ;
  • backend/src/services/gof-service.ts ;
  • integration in backend/src/routes/admin/index.ts;
  • API call on the front-end;
  • adaptation of PdfsPage.tsx.

The direction of development is consistent: GOF has begun to move beyond a simple local folder to become a feed visible from KEREDIT, without shifting the business authority. KEREDIT remains the back office, whilst GOF remains the development environment.

We will need to revisit this issue with caution: it touches on PDF processing, and therefore lies at the interface between the editor, admin, payload, worker and workshop machine.

Beta tests

We also tidied up several E2E tests today.

The aim was not to expand the product, but to bring the tests into line with the current branding and store interfaces:

  • admin assets;
  • clipart;
  • smoke editor;
  • text link;
  • insertion from panels;
  • photo block;
  • text block;
  • logo customisation.

The feedback received regarding the logo project has been positive:

  • pnpm typecheck ;
  • pnpm lint with a previously known warning on UsersPage.tsx;
  • PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=adresse locale pnpm exec playwright test e2e/personalization-logo.spec.ts --workers=1 ;
  • pnpm build during the validation of the first logo commit.

What this tells us about the beta

The beta doesn’t need a perfect logo to exist.

But it does need to ensure that the small, visible details do not give the impression of being cobbled together. A square logo when the interface promises a round one is not a technical issue; it sends the wrong message about the product.

So 2 June was useful for one simple reason: it restored consistency to the visible interfaces, whilst continuing to lay the groundwork for PDF/GOF.

The goal remains the same:

  • not to expand the scope before we have any client partners;
  • to keep postcard as the priority beta product;
  • to stabilise what the user actually sees;
  • let the PDF project move forward through contracts and evidence, not through improvisation.

Follow-up

Recommended priorities following today’s session:

  1. check that logo customisation remains correct after reloading and across all platforms;
  2. do not reopen the general theming under the pretext of the logo;
  3. version control or save GOF properly, as dépôt local gof now contains application code without an active Git repository;
  4. resume work on GOF via a clear contract between KEREDIT and the development team;
  5. re-run the full postcard workflow before sending out external invitations;
  6. keep the E2E tests as a beta safety net, not as a permanent cosmetic overhaul.

The day began with documentation and ended with a visible detail being fixed. That’s often what the beta approach is all about: making the parts that will be seen first less fragile.

body.source:
Horaires de session

  • Agent utilisé : aucun pendant la journée du 1er juin ; billet rédige rétrospectivement avec Codex le 2 juin 2026
  • Environnement principal : non utilise pour l’atelier Krampouz/KEREDIT ce jour-la
  • Date : lundi 1er juin 2026
  • Branche : dev
  • Version application connue : 0.6.49
  • Version plugin WordPress/WooCommerce de référence : 0.1.27
  • Dernier SHA connu avant reprise du 2 juin : 3d4400e
  • Amplitude observée par les commits : aucun commit observé le 1er juin 2026
  • Temps actif estimé : 0 h côté atelier
  • Commits principaux pousses : aucun Il n’y à pas eu de chantier Krampouz/KEREDIT le 1er juin. Pas de session atelier. Pas de replay du parcours postcard. Pas de correction de dernière minute. Pas de validation PDF, WooCommerce, plugin, prix ou reprise projet. Ce billet existe quand même, pour une raison simple : un journal utile doit aussi savoir dire quand il ne s’est rien passé. Le silence non documente finit toujours par ressembler à un trou, puis à une incertitude. Ici, le fait important est clair : le 1er juin n’a pas été une journée de travail atelier.
  • Temps cumulé minimal depuis le début du journal : environ 368h48+, inchange

Ce que cela confirme

Le 1er juin était auparavant une date symbolique d’ouverture possible. Après la décision du 29 mai, il ne fallait plus la traiter comme une date active d’entrée clients amis.

La position reste donc cohérente :

  • pas d’ouverture bêta clients amis le 1er juin ;
  • semaine du 1er au 7 juin gardée pour stabilisation poste, outillage et reprise propre ;
  • cible clients amis repoussée au 8 juin 2026, sauf blocage réel constate ;
  • postcard reste le produit prioritaire de la bêta fermée ;
  • GOF reste le futur chantier forge PDF, mais sans déplacer le journal dans un deuxième blog.

La journée n’a rien ajouté au produit. Elle n’a pas non plus abime le plan.

Vérification

Vérification retrospective faite le 2 juin :

  • git log --since='2026-06-01 00:00' --until='2026-06-01 23:59' --oneline --decorate : aucun commit ;
  • versions package.json et frontend/package.json : 0.6.49 ;
  • branche courante au moment de la rédaction : dev.

Aucune vérification runtime n’est associée au 1er juin, puisqu’il n’y à pas eu de session atelier à valider.

Reprise

Priorités recommandées pour la suite :

  1. reprendre par un git status --short --branch avant tout chantier ;
  2. vérifier que le poste, Codex, les accès et le runtime local sont stables ;
  3. rejouer le parcours postcard complet avant toute invitation clients amis ;
  4. garder le 8 juin comme horizon prudent, pas comme promesse automatique ;
  5. ne pas compenser la journée blanche par un chantier trop large le lendemain.

Parfois, la bonne trace projet est courte : hier, je n’etais pas à l’atelier.

title.source: Day 71 – A day away from the studio

items.title: Day 71 – A day away from the studio

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin on the left, code in the centre, Codex terminal on the right
  • Date: Friday 29 May 2026
  • Branch: dev
  • Application version at the end of the day: 0.6.49
  • Reference WordPress/WooCommerce plugin version: 0.1.27
  • Latest known SHA on dev: 69c914b
  • Activity observed via commits: no new application commits observed on that day; in dépôt local gof, PDF build files modified between 11:09 and 18:04
  • Estimated active time: cannot be accurately measured from the Git logs, but the day involved a combination of interruptions, scheduling decisions and the initial structuring of GOF
  • Main commits pushed: no application commits on 29 May; GOF is not yet a local Git repository 29 May was supposed to be a Go/No-Go review day. It was, but not as planned. Instead of a calm review of the beta process, the day mainly served as a reminder of one simple point: when the workstation shuts down, overheats and disconnects three times in the same day, it is no longer just a minor annoyance. It becomes a project risk.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 368h48+, unchanged due to lack of useful commit records

Three outages

The workstation suffered three interruptions:

  • a general power cut linked to the electricity grid;
  • two outages caused by the machine overheating.

It’s not just a nuisance. On KEREDIT, a workstation outage can disrupt far more than just concentration:

  • Codex sessions cut short;
  • lost debug contexts;
  • browser, terminal, backend or worker that needs to be checked again;
  • risk of mistaking a local glitch for a genuine application bug;
  • extra fatigue at precisely the moment when the beta requires a clear head.

The project already has enough real issues to deal with: e-postcards, shopping basket recovery, workshop support, PDFs, assets, the WordPress plugin and product data. Adding an unstable machine to the beta cycle would be counterproductive.

Hardware decision

The result was concrete: an order for a Mac mini M4 Pro.

This isn’t a matter of fancying a fancy setup. It’s a decision regarding local infrastructure. The workstation has become part of the critical path, just like the VPS or the WordPress plugin.

Next week will therefore involve migrating the environment:

  • development tools;
  • local repositories and secrets;
  • Docker / pnpm / Node;
  • VPS and GitHub access;
  • Codex configuration;
  • personal skills and project skills;
  • working habits relating to VS Code, the terminal, the browser and screenshots.

Between excitement and added stress, we need to accept that this transition will take up some time. Treating it as a simple ‘in-between’ task would be the surest way to ruin the beta.

GOF: the future PDF forge

The other important thread from 29 May wasn’t in the Krampouz repo itself. It was in:

dépôt local gof

GOF, which is beginning to take shape as the future PDF workshop forge for KEREDIT.

The proposal has already set out several key structural choices:

  • workshop machinegof with a static IP[adresse LAN];
  • Target installation: Ubuntu Server + Docker Compose;
  • local dashboard at 8080;
  • Local Redis to manage a job queue;
  • Nginx Proxy Manager for secure HTTPS access via forge.keredit.com;
  • persistent volumes for logs, Redis, proxy, fonts and data;
  • Dedicated NVMe for fast storage at cache, work, tmp and output-staging;
  • Node.js base ready for a native Cairo/Fabric PDF renderer, without Puppeteer.

The GOF documents created or consolidated also describe the implementation:

  • README.md : GOF’s role as a local PDF forge;
  • docs/runbook-installation-ubuntu.md : Ubuntu reinstallation, bootstrapping, deployment, checks;
  • docs/securite-atelier.md : firewall, LAN-only, blocked ports;
  • docs/exposition-https-autonome.md : DNS, Freebox Pro NAT, HTTPS, Basic Auth;
  • docs/operations-gof.md : control commands;
  • docs/dns-lan-stock2.md : LAN DNS incident with STOCK2 and cache NXDOMAIN;
  • docs/audit-truenas-[adresse LAN].md : treating the old TrueNAS as a storage appliance, not as a practical application host.

This is a key principle for KEREDIT: GOF must not read the internal tables directly. KEREDIT remains the authority for commands, projects, templates and assets. GOF must consume a complete, versioned PDF payload, then produce the rendered artefacts.

PDF processing is also moving in a more sound direction: no large PNG images pasted into a PDF, no Puppeteer eating up all the RAM. What is needed is a genuine production-quality PDF, with text and shapes preserved where possible, HD images rendered from R2, fonts embedded, and vector rendering via Cairo/Fabric. Put simply: the PDF must remain a page-based document, not a giant screenshot.

Blog decision: we must not start a second blog for GOF. As long as GOF exists as KEREDIT’s PDF forge, its progress must be reported here, in the Krampouz/KEREDIT blog, with an explicit link to dépôt local gof.

Beta decision

Today’s decision is therefore:

No-Go for opening up to partner clients on 1 June 2026. A cautious one-week postponement, with Wave 1 now targeted for 8 June 2026.

This postponement does not change the product itself. It changes the timetable.

The scope remains deliberately narrow:

  • postcard as a priority product;
  • WooCommerce for product listings, the shopping basket and payment;
  • KEREDIT as the business authority for prices, formats, quantities and options;
  • possible workshop support adjustments;
  • photo_print and fine_art_print will provide support in the background, without making any broad promises.

1 June can remain a symbolic date and an internal milestone. But it must no longer be the date on which partner clients are brought into an environment that we know will need to be migrated shortly afterwards.

What this changes in the plan

The week of 1 to 7 June becomes a week of stabilisation and workstation migration:

  1. moving the development environment to a reliable machine;
  2. migrate Codex, the skills and access rights;
  3. check that the repository, the local runtime and the VPS are all in sync;
  4. re-run the full ‘postcard’ workflow after migration;
  5. only invite beta testers once local support has returned to normal.

The delay is frustrating, but sensible. A beta for friends and family doesn’t need a perfect product. It needs a reliable ability to respond when something goes wrong.

Yesterday, the signal was clear: it’s not yet the right time to bring in external testers.

Resumption

Recommended priorities:

  1. document the postponement in the beta plan;
  2. prepare a short checklist for the migration of workstations, Codex and skills;
  3. version control or, at the very least, properly back up GOF before expanding it;
  4. explicitly link the future Krampouz PDF payload to the GOF consumer;
  5. check the current status of dev before starting any new work;
  6. run the ‘postcard’ cycle again once the new environment is ready;
  7. keep 8 June as the new target date, unless a genuine obstacle is identified.

The day did not advance the editor’s development, but it did prevent a mistake: forcing a beta release out of a desire to stick to a deadline, when the local working infrastructure first needed to be secured.

items.title: Day 70 – When the job itself becomes a risk

body.source:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin on the left, code in the centre, Codex terminal on the right
  • Date: Thursday 28 May 2026
  • Branch: dev
  • Application version at the end of the day: 0.6.49
  • Reference WordPress/WooCommerce plugin version: 0.1.27
  • Latest known SHA on dev: 2ea8f9c8b0005b1d107cfcaf33190a4552a4fa7c
  • Duration observed from commits: 10:17 -> 13:43, i.e. at least 3 hours 26 minutes
  • Estimated active time: approximately 3 hours 30 minutes to 5 hours, including a product review, checks, followed by tool-based documentation
  • Main commits pushed:
    • fdcb513 - docs: document codex transition and blog metadata
    • 2ea8f9c - docs: add poubelle cleanup workflow The day did not add any major visible feature to the editor. Instead, it neatly wrapped up what had been started the previous day: a potential KEREDIT beta on 1 June, provided it is not turned into a public launch, and a repository that must remain readable whilst the pressure mounts. The guiding principle was simple: make small decisions, document accurately, and clean up without breaking anything.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 368h48+

1 June Go/No-Go decision

The morning began with a decision-making meeting regarding the 1 June launch.

The verdict remains deliberately cautious: a limited go, not a full-scale launch. The appropriate scope is a controlled beta for friends and clients, with postcard as the priority product, WooCommerce as the shopping basket and payment system, and KEREDIT as the business authority for quantities, formats and prices.

The checks and reviewed documents all pointed in this direction:

  • docs/produit/ouverture-beta-keredit-juin-2026.md ;
  • docs/produit/roadmap.md ;
  • the post dated 27 May;
  • dev’s local status was clean;
  • pnpm dev:status ;
  • pnpm typecheck ;
  • pnpm lint ;
  • public checks on the KEREDIT API, the theme, the OOBLIK product page and the plugin manifest.

Practical conclusion: the 1 June beta is credible for a select few, but it remains conditional upon the full user journey being re-run between 29 and 31 May:

produit OOBLIK -> éditeur KEREDIT -> prix -> panier Woo -> retour édition -> commande -> backoffice/support

The known React warning in frontend/src/components/admin/UsersPage.tsx remains non-blocking, but we must keep an eye on it.

Codex log and transition

Today’s first commit has made the new approach to documentation explicit.

Main additions:

  • creation of .codex-skills/blog/SKILL.md;
  • addition of a transition note to docs/blog/transition-claude-codex-2026.md;
  • enrichment of the blog index with cross-cutting notes;
  • metadata added to older posts;
  • updating docs/guides/commandes-dev.md, docs/HOME.md and BIBLIOTHEQUE.md.

The aim was not to rewrite history. It was to ensure the long-term sustainability of how the log should be maintained now that Codex is becoming the primary tool: dated entries, recorded timings, commits, validations, human context where relevant, and a maintained index.

This is important so that we can pick up where we left off tomorrow without having to trawl through scattered records.

Trash workflow

The second commit added a reversible clean-up workflow.

New features:

  • creation of .codex-skills/poubelle/SKILL.md;
  • addition of the `.codex-skills/poubelle/scripts/audit-tmp.sh` script;
  • creation of `poubelle/`;
  • creation of poubelle-historique.md;
  • updated docs/HOME.md and BIBLIOTHEQUE.md.

The rule is deliberately conservative: we do not delete the project’s history. We remove obsolete files from the current read path, retain their relative location under poubelle/, and record the reason why.

The first pass moved two old reports from docs/analyse/print-ooblik-20260330-* to:

poubelle/docs/analyse/

These files were no longer active workspaces. Keeping them in the main directory structure introduced clutter every time the documentation was browsed.

What this update really changes

The beta is no broader than it was yesterday. And that is precisely the point.

We’ve made it clear that the right approach isn’t to open things up further, but to make recovery and auditing more reliable:

  • the beta verdict is bounded;
  • the log has a versioned user guide;
  • the transition from Claude Code to Codex is documented;
  • future clean-ups follow a protocol;
  • old artefacts can be moved out of the way without disappearing.

This isn’t the sort of day that makes an impression in a demo. It’s the sort of day that saves you from wasting two hours in three weeks’ time wondering why an old report or a note contradicts the current status.

Checks

Checks carried out during the day:

  • pnpm dev:status : backend healthy, frontend reachable, worker active;
  • pnpm typecheck : OK;
  • pnpm lint : OK, with the known warningUsersPage.tsx;
  • https://ooblik.keredit.com/api/health : OK;
  • https://ooblik.keredit.com/api/theme : OK;
  • OOBLIK test product page: HTTP 200;
  • keredit-connector plugin manifest: version 0.1.27.

For documentation commits, the main risk is not runtime-related. It lies instead in the consistency of paths and indexing, hence the updates to docs/HOME.md, BIBLIOTHEQUE.md and docs/blog/_index.md.

To be continued tomorrow

Recommended priorities:

  1. run through the entire beta test again under controlled conditions;
  2. correct or explicitly acknowledge the warning at UsersPage.tsx;
  3. check PDF regeneration / support fixes on a real project;
  4. prepare a short message for client friends;
  5. use the ‘poubelle’ workflow only with supporting evidence, not merely as a cosmetic organiser.

The day was quieter than 27 May, but productive: the product remains beta-oriented, and the repository is starting to better manage its own version history.

title.source: Day 69 – Keeping the beta small and the memory clean

items.title: Day 69 – Keeping the beta small and the memory clean

body.source:
Session timetable

  • System used: Codex
  • Date: Wednesday 27 May 2026
  • Branch: dev
  • Application version at the end of the day: 0.6.49
  • WordPress/WooCommerce plugin version at the end of the day: 0.1.27
  • Latest SHA deployed on the VPS: 8f329c30c45e7f907df340d59d84249ac5443ecd
  • Time span covered by commits: 09:02 -> 19:37, i.e. at least 10 hours 35 minutes
  • Estimated active time: approximately 8 to 10 hours, with many short cycles of code → deployment → live testing
  • Main commits pushed:
    • a506a06 - fix: sync woo quantities from keredit
    • de9fe9b - feat: add admin data transfer exports
    • d714b43 - Fix admin product transfer refresh
    • 030ba39 - Allow legacy paper pricing parameter
    • c522609 - Add admin Woo REST checkout credentials
    • 914d436 - Route editor checkout through Woo cart bridge
    • 62ed77f - Lock Keredit cart quantities
    • 0629663 - Add Keredit cart edit link
    • 18493cf - Add admin order filters
    • 856eb2b - Fix support asset access and order search
    • 23987a9 - Keep admin order filters focused
    • 8f329c3 - Hide checkout during support corrections The day was less visually spectacular than the authentication day, but it transformed KEREDIT from a trendy editor into a fully-fledged beta-testable e-commerce experience. The overarching principle: KEREDIT must be the business logic engine, WooCommerce must handle sales and payments, and the development team must be able to take over without having to tinker with the code.
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approx. 365h22+

Progress: KEREDIT takes back control

The first block corrected a significant contractual error.

WooCommerce was still launching projects with a quantity of `1`, whereas the KEREDIT product `Carte postale` had started at `8 exemplaires`. The price therefore logically failed with `400 Bad Request`.

The fix has aligned the data flow:

  • the WooCommerce product reads the authorised quantities from KEREDIT;
  • the editor starts with a valid quantity;
  • the WooCommerce basket displays the quantity printed by KEREDIT;
  • the standard WooCommerce quantity is locked for KEREDIT lines;
  • the customer can return to edit their order from the basket, change the format or quantity, and then place the order again.

This point is central to the beta. It prevents a dangerous discrepancy between the product page, editor, price and basket.

Product data: export/import to avoid confusion between code and database

The live test highlighted another point of confusion: the deployment included the code, but not the local data on prices, formats, paper types and workshop attributes.

On ooblik.keredit.com, some products were therefore empty or incomplete even though the local system was correctly configured.

The Produits & Prix back office now features an export/import workflow to transfer product and workshop data:

  • export of local product data;
  • import to the VPS;
  • correction of the admin refresh after import;
  • correct populating of workshop attributes in the product record;
  • compatibility with the old paper=invercote_300 setting.

After import and redeployment, the price went live again. This was the first real e-commerce hurdle of the day.

Woo integrations: the client will be able to configure their keys

The Intégrations back office has been enhanced so that the WooCommerce integration can be utilised by a KEREDIT client.

What has changed:

  • Woo REST credentials configurable via the KEREDIT admin panel;
  • encryption of secrets via INTEGRATION_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY;
  • Woo connection test;
  • explicit activation of the WooCommerce command;
  • UX distinction between mandatory REST keys and optional webhook secrets.

The key point: KEREDIT must not depend on any invisible manipulation carried out by us via SSH. The back office must explain and manage the configuration.

WooCommerce basket: the first customer cycle works

The ‘Commander’ button in the editor now calls KEREDIT, which adds the line to the WooCommerce basket and then redirects to OOBLIK.

The workflow has been validated in production:

  1. open an OOBLIK product;
  2. launch the KEREDIT editor;
  3. create/edit a postcard;
  4. calculate the price;
  5. place an order;
  6. add it to the OOBLIK basket;
  7. view the KEREDIT line item showing the design, format, print run and paper type;
  8. click on ‘éditer’ from the basket;
  9. change the format or quantity;
  10. return to the basket with the updated price.

The basket should no longer display the WooCommerce quantity selector on these lines. The business-specific quantity is managed by KEREDIT.

Admin commands and support fixes

The Commandes page in the KEREDIT back office can now be used to track projects with a WooCommerce order.

Today’s additions:

  • search;
  • filters;
  • sorting;
  • pagination;
  • dynamic search without pressing Enter;
  • fix for the focus bug that prevented users from typing more than one letter;
  • opening the project in support edit mode.

Support mode has also been secured in terms of assets.

Problem encountered: when opening a client project from the admin panel, certain images displayed:

/api/assets/:id/url 404 Asset non trouvé

Cause: the support admin could open the project, but could not necessarily resolve the URL of the client asset attached to the project.

Fix:

  • admin/editor access authorised for assets linked to a project within the same tenant;
  • Live verification of an asset URL via 200;
  • ‘Commander’ button hidden in support correction mode;
  • retention of Sauvegarder and Régénérer PDF.

Product decision: when the workshop corrects a client project, it must not place an order on the client’s behalf.

Deployments and validation

Several short VPS deployments were carried out, with version increments up to 0.6.49.

The day’s checks included:

  • pnpm test:backend after asset support corrections;
  • pnpm typecheck ;
  • pnpm lint ;
  • VPS deployments with backups;
  • public smoke tests;
  • live tests on https://ooblik.com/impressions/test-krampouz/;
  • price testing;
  • shopping basket test;
  • test of editing and returning items from the basket;
  • testing of order visibility in the KEREDIT back office;
  • support correction test with project images.

A known front-end warning still needs to be resolved regarding ‘UsersPage.tsx’, but it did not prevent today’s workflows from proceeding.

Useful issues

The day mainly revealed discrepancies in the terms and conditions:

  • Woo quantity 1 versus KEREDIT quantity 8;
  • local product data not present in production;
  • Woo integration not sufficiently clear in the back office;
  • Woo shopping basket still attempting to modify a business quantity;
  • a support fix that opened the project but not always the assets;
  • order filter that lost focus with every keystroke.

These issues are positive signs ahead of the beta: they arose during a real customer journey, not in an abstract scenario. And they have been resolved in line with the product’s design, not by workarounds.

Beta update on the evening of 27 May

Yes, we’re in a much better position for the 1 June beta.

We’re not yet at the stage of a wide public launch. However, a controlled ‘friends and family’ beta is now a realistic prospect:

  • the ‘produit -> éditeur -> prix -> panier’ shopping journey exists;
  • the customer can return to edit their order from the shopping basket;
  • the workshop can view orders in KEREDIT;
  • support can open and amend a customer project;
  • quantities and prices are now managed by KEREDIT;
  • product data can be transferred correctly between the local system and the VPS.

What remains to be validated before launch:

  • re-run a complete, error-free workflow, from the OOBLIK product through to the Woo order;
  • check the PDF regeneration for support on a live project;
  • confirm the order/webhook status if we wish to use it in the beta;
  • document the product data import runbook before each thorough test;
  • keep the launch limited to a few friendly clients, no more.

My recommendation: proceed with caution for 1 June, provided the review on 29–31 May confirms a full cycle without any blocking incidents. The appropriate scope is postcard + Woo basket + support fixes. No marketing expansion, no multi-product promises.

Back to work tomorrow

Short-term priorities:

  1. re-run the full end-to-end live user journey;
  2. check PDF/support regeneration;
  3. check that production product data is saved and exportable;
  4. clear the latest non-blocking warnings that interfere with playback;
  5. prepare the beta announcement for partner clients.

Today, it was still around 32 degrees outside. We’re certainly feeling the strain, but the product has reached a significant milestone: the sales journey is no longer just a theoretical concept.

description.source: Beta consolidation day: KEREDIT master quantities, WooCommerce shopping basket integration, product data import/export, Woo integrations, admin orders, support fixes and VPS deployments.

items.title: Day 68 – The KEREDIT commerce journey is now available for testing

body.source:
Horaires de session

  • Agent utilisé : Codex
  • Date : mardi 26 mai 2026
  • Branche : dev
  • Version repo en fin de journée : 0.6.39
  • Version plugin WordPress/WooCommerce en fin de journée : 0.1.23
  • Amplitude observée par les commits : 09:06 -> 19:56, soit 10 h 50 minimum
  • Temps actif estimé : environ 9 h 30 à 11 h, en comptant les validations live, les diagnostics WordPress, les déploiements VPS et les reprises de procédure
  • Commits principaux pousses :
    • fcd282d - docs: add 2026-05-25 backend refactor journal
    • bc3eca7 - refactor: extract woocommerce checkout facade
    • 60da70f - fix: repair product workshop attribute migrations
    • 295b973 - feat: add Better Auth beta foundation
    • 8bdec5c - feat: harden auth and admin user management
    • f05bd66 - feat: connect editor checkout and Woo support bridge
    • 97efe7f - fix: install openssl in docker images for prisma
    • 910946a - fix: enforce wordpress plugin release publishing
    • 4478548 - fix: keep legacy wordpress admin plugin urls working La journée a commencé sur la fin du chantier P1 backend et s’est terminée sur un incident de procédure plugin qui a été transformé en garde-fou exécutable. Le fil rouge était le même que la veille : moins de zones implicites, plus de contrats que le code peut vérifier. Sauf qu’aujourd’hui le sujet n’était pas seulement l’architecture backend. Il a touché l’authentification, les utilisateurs admin, le checkout éditeur, le VPS, le plugin WordPress, et surtout la façon dont une release devient visible en production.
  • Temps cumulé minimal depuis le début du journal : environ 354h47+

Fin du P1 backend et WooCommerce service

Le premier travail a été de terminer la suite logique du P1 backend.

Après pricing, assets et print jobs, backend/src/routes/woocommerce.ts a été allégée en sortant le workflow métier dans backend/src/services/woocommerce-service.ts.

Le service porte maintenant les use cases importants :

  • création de commande checkout depuis un projet ;
  • consommation de token de lancement Woo ;
  • webhook de commande confirmée ;
  • reprise, duplication et suppression de projets client ;
  • lock de checkout pour éviter les doubles commandes.

La route reste responsable du HTTP : schémas, status codes, headers, auth intégration et cookies. Les décisions métier sont dans le service.

Ce lot a aussi réparé des migrations d’attributs atelier et de processus MISKISS qui bloquaient les contrats Prisma. Ce n’est pas glamour, mais c’est essentiel : une bêta ne peut pas dépendre d’un historique Prisma approximatif.

Le P1 backend a ensuite été merge sur dev via PR.

Better Auth : socle bêta et Google OAuth

Le gros chantier du milieu de journée a été l’authentification.

L’objectif n’était pas de remplacer brutalement l’ancien /api/auth. Le choix a été plus prudent : ajouter Better Auth sur une surface isolée /api/auth-v2/*, puis construire un pont vers la session KEREDIT existante.

Ce qui a été posé :

  • models Prisma better_auth_* ;
  • configuration backend/src/lib/better-auth.ts avec adapter Prisma ;
  • Google OAuth optionnel ;
  • route /api/auth-v2/keredit/session pour convertir une session Better Auth valide en session KEREDIT ;
  • route de config OAuth pour masquer Google quand les secrets ne sont pas présents ;
  • preflight local pnpm auth:preflight ;
  • documentation dans docs/architecture/auth-roadmap-better-auth-2026.md.

Le test local Google a fait apparaître un state_mismatch, puis le parcours a été corrigé côté environnement/cookies jusqu’à obtenir une connexion fonctionnelle.

Sur le VPS, il a fallu ajouter explicitement les variables Better Auth dans le compose. Le login Google backoffice a ensuite été validé en live sur ooblik.keredit.com.

Décision produit importante : pendant la bêta, la création publique de compte reste fermée. Les comptes sont créés depuis le backoffice. Le bouton Creer un compte a donc été retiré, et le public signup Better Auth est rejeté côté backend.

Utilisateurs admin : enfin un vrai outil

Le backoffice Utilisateurs était trop pauvre pour administrer KEREDIT sérieusement.

Le chantier a ajouté une vraie gestion opérationnelle :

  • liste avec recherche, filtres, tri et sélection multiple ;
  • édition utilisateur ;
  • changement de rôle ;
  • reset ou initialisation de mot de passe ;
  • rattachement et lecture des projets accessibles ;
  • suppression protégée ;
  • actions batch ;
  • vraie implémentation reset password, pas un placeholder bêta.

L’UX a été revue pendant la session :

  • champ recherche corrigé ;
  • drawer latéral remplace par une modale centrée ;
  • projets présentes de façon plus compacte ;
  • ouverture des projets client dans un nouvel onglet ;
  • confirmation de suppression via notre modale, pas window.confirm.

Ce lot a aussi clarifié une règle produit : KEREDIT est l’admin des clients qui utilisent l’application. OOBLIK est le premier client, mais l’interface doit rester capable de gérer d’autres comptes, rôles et projets.

Le pont OOBLIK : corriger un projet client depuis KEREDIT

Une question produit a structuré la suite : si un client OOBLIK commande une carte postale puis signale une faute, où doit-on corriger ?

La décision retenue : la correction du projet se fait dans KEREDIT, pas dans WordPress. WordPress/WooCommerce reste le canal commerce, commande et paiement. KEREDIT reste l’atelier de création, correction et support.

Le code a donc ajouté un pont support :

  • backend/src/services/admin-project-support-service.ts ;
  • contexte support Woo dans les routes admin projets et commandes ;
  • liens visibles dans les pages admin KEREDIT ;
  • metabox KEREDIT dans les commandes WooCommerce quand une commande porte _keredit_project_id.

Le but est simple : depuis une commande Woo, OOBLIK doit pouvoir ouvrir le projet KEREDIT correspondant et corriger rapidement.

Éditeur : prix visible et bouton Commander

La fin de journée produit a touché l’éditeur.

Le panneau de propriétés affichait encore un mini récap prix redondant. Le prix total a été remonté dans le header, à côté de l’action de commande.

Le nouveau flux :

  • le header montre Total XX,XX EUR ;
  • le bouton principal est Commander ;
  • Sauvegarder quitte le header et passé dans la ligne de menu, aligne à droite ;
  • le panneau de propriétés gardé format, nom, quantité et options, mais plus le récap panier.

Plusieurs corrections UX ont suivi :

  • bouton Commander invisible au hover ;
  • état disable trop blanc ;
  • libellé qui clignote entre Sauvegarder et Sauve ;
  • alignement et contraste terracotta ;
  • suppression du tooltip inutile Commander ce projet.

Le hook frontend/src/hooks/useEditorCheckout.ts centralise maintenant devis, options par défaut et action checkout. Le bouton appelle /api/projects/:id/add-to-cart, puis redirige vers WooCommerce.

En local, le checkout échouait avec une erreur 500 parce que les credentials Woo locaux étaient des placeholders. Ce n’était pas un bug du code : le VPS devait être testé avec les vrais secrets.

Déploiement VPS et warning Prisma/OpenSSL

Un déploiement VPS a été lancé pour tester le parcours en production.

Source de vérité :

  • branche dev ;
  • SHA f05bd66ad959, puis 97efe7f91479 après correctif Docker ;
  • version 0.6.37, puis 0.6.38.

Le deploy nominal deploy/manual-vps-local.sh a construit les images sur le VPS, applique Prisma, seed, redémarre backend/worker/frontend et vérifié :

  • https://ooblik.keredit.com/ ;
  • https://krampouz.ooblik.com/ ;
  • /api/health ;
  • /api/theme.

Un avertissement Prisma/OpenSSL est apparu dans les conteneurs Node. Il aurait été facile de le repousser à “après bêta”. Marc a refusé, à raison.

La correction a installé openssl et ca-certificates dans les stages Docker Node :

  • Dockerfile.backend stage deps ;
  • Dockerfile.backend stage runtime ;
  • Dockerfile.frontend stage deps, car le build frontend installe aussi le workspace backend et déclenche prisma generate.

Validation :

  • build Docker local backend/frontend ;
  • npx prisma generate dans l’image runtime sans warning ;
  • redéploiement VPS ;
  • logs backend/worker relus sans prisma:warn, failed to detect ou openssl.

Plugin WordPress : la procédure devait devenir exécutable

Le plus gros rappel à l’ordre de la journée est venu du plugin WordPress.

Le code plugin avait été modifié pour le support commande Woo, mais aucune mise à jour n’apparaissait dans le backoffice OOBLIK.

Cause initiale : le plugin source était reste en version 0.1.20. Si le manifest public dit déjà 0.1.20 et que WordPress à 0.1.20, WordPress ne proposera jamais d’update.

Cause réelle plus profonde : ooblik.com utilisait encore l’ancien slug installe krampouz-connector, alors que la publication récente visait surtout keredit-connector. On publiait le mauvais canal pour l’installation active.

La correction a été volontairement plus dure qu’un patch :

  • création de pnpm plugin:publish ;
  • lint PHP ;
  • build ZIP ;
  • alignement manifest/checksum ;
  • upload sur updates.ooblik.com ;
  • publication du canal canonique keredit-connector ;
  • publication du canal legacy krampouz-connector tant que le site live n’a pas migré ;
  • vérification checksum public ;
  • purge caches WordPress ;
  • vérification WP-CLI.

Le script de deploy VPS contrôle maintenant les changements sous wordpress-plugin/keredit-connector/. Si le plugin à change sans version publiée, le déploiement refuse de continuer.

AGENTS.md, le skill .codex-skills/wp-plugin-release, le guide WooCommerce et BIBLIOTHEQUE.md ont été mis à jour : une modification plugin n’est plus une simple édition source, c’est une release.

Incident de migration plugin et correction 0.1.23

En activant la nouvelle version, WordPress a affiché :

Desole, vous n’avez pas l’autorisation d’accéder à cette page.

La page ouverte était admin.php?page=krampouz-editor.

Le problème n’était pas le compte utilisateur. C’était un slug admin legacy non déclaré par le nouveau plugin. Après la migration, WordPress gardait ou ouvrait encore l’ancienne URL, mais le plugin ne l’enregistrait plus.

La version 0.1.23 a restauré les alias :

  • page=krampouz-editor redirige vers page=keredit ;
  • page=krampouz-connector redirige vers les réglages techniques ;
  • les options live ont été migrées vers keredit_connector_settings ;
  • le plugin actif sur ooblik.com est maintenant keredit-connector, version 0.1.23.

Vérification WP-CLI finale :

keredit-connector,KEREDIT,active,0.1.23,none

Complément tardif : test live et quantité Woo/KEREDIT

Après le close-out initial, un test en situation sur le produit OOBLIK test krampouz a révélé un autre problème de contrat commerce.

Le produit n’était pas perdu. Il existait toujours côté WordPress, mais son permalink courant était :

https://ooblik.com/impressions/test-krampouz/

L’ancienne URL /produit/test-krampouz/ redirigeait vers ce nouveau slug, et le produit restait marqué en visibilité catalogue cachée. Les metas legacy _krampouz_connector_* et les nouvelles metas _keredit_connector_* étaient présentes, donc le changement Krampouz/KEREDIT n’avait pas efface le mapping.

Le vrai bug était ailleurs : le lancement WooCommerce créait un projet KEREDIT avec selected_quantity = 1, puis l’éditeur appelait :

/api/projects/:id/pricing?...&quantity=1...

Or le produit KEREDIT Carte postale impose une règle de quantités :

min = 8
default = 8
values = [8, 16, 24, 48, 100, 200, 500]

Le 400 Bad Request était donc logique : KEREDIT refusait une quantité invalide. La faille était dans l’alignement produit : WooCommerce envoyait sa quantité de ligne par défaut (1) comme si c’était la quantité d’exemplaires atelier.

Décision de contrat prise en fin de soirée :

  • KEREDIT est la source de vérité des quantités imprimées ;
  • le produit WooCommerce doit recevoir les quantités autorisées depuis KEREDIT ;
  • le plugin doit synchroniser automatiquement la règle quantité du produit KEREDIT ;
  • la fiche produit Woo ne doit plus laisser partir 1 si KEREDIT attend 8, 16, 24, etc. ;
  • le backend KEREDIT doit rester défensif et refuser ou corriger toute quantité Woo invalide.

Un correctif local a été commencé sur cette base :

  • nouvelle route backend /api/woocommerce/products/:productId/config pour exposer la config produit KEREDIT au plugin ;
  • nouveau module plugin class-product-sync.php pour synchroniser et cacher la règle de quantité sur le produit Woo ;
  • transformation du champ quantité Woo en liste des valeurs KEREDIT autorisées ;
  • protection backend pour ne plus créer un projet depuis Woo avec selected_quantity=1 quand la règle produit demande 8 ;
  • correction frontend pour rebasculer les anciens projets invalides vers une quantité autorisée.

État au moment de l’interruption poste :

  • version locale préparée : application 0.6.40, plugin 0.1.24 ;
  • ZIP plugin keredit-connector-0.1.24.zip construit localement ;
  • manifest local 0.1.24 mis à jour avec checksum ;
  • upload vers updates.ooblik.com interrompu avant publication ;
  • aucun commit ni deploy VPS effectué après a14b027.

Ce complément change la conclusion produit : le parcours client complet ne doit pas seulement vérifier bouton, éditeur et checkout. Il doit aussi vérifier que la fiche WooCommerce et KEREDIT parlent exactement la même langue sur les quantités, les formats, les options et le prix.

Vérifications de la journée

Les checks lances pendant la journée ont inclus :

  • pnpm typecheck ;
  • pnpm --filter backend typecheck ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend typecheck ;
  • pnpm --filter backend lint ;
  • pnpm --filter frontend lint ;
  • pnpm --filter backend test -- src/services/admin-project-support-service.test.ts ;
  • pnpm build ;
  • pnpm plugin:lint ;
  • pnpm plugin:publish ;
  • build Docker backend/frontend local ;
  • génération Prisma dans image runtime backend ;
  • deploy VPS avec smoke public ;
  • vérification logs backend/worker ;
  • vérification manifests et ZIP publics avec checksums ;
  • vérification WP-CLI plugin, options migrées et slugs admin legacy.

Un warning lint frontend reste connu sur UsersPage.tsx autour d’une dépendance useEffect. Il n’a pas bloqué la journée, mais il doit être nettoyé pour réduire le bruit.

Auto-critique

La journée montre deux choses.

D’abord, les gros chantiers avancent bien quand les frontières sont explicites : route/service, auth provider/session KEREDIT, WordPress commerce/KEREDIT atelier, deploy app/release plugin.

Ensuite, une procédure dans la doc n’est pas une procédure fiable. Tant que le deploy pouvait passer alors qu’un plugin avait changé sans release, le système était fragile. Le bon correctif n’était pas de “penser à le faire”. Le bon correctif était de faire échouer le script.

Le même principe vaut pour les migrations legacy : on ne peut pas supposer que le live à déjà le nouveau slug. Tant que ooblik.com portait encore krampouz-connector, le canal legacy devait rester vivant.

État pour demain

Le socle est meilleur qu’au matin :

  • Better Auth est posé et Google backoffice fonctionne ;
  • la création publique de compte est fermée pour la bêta ;
  • l’admin utilisateurs devient utilisable ;
  • l’éditeur sait afficher prix et commander ;
  • le VPS sert 0.6.38 aujourd’hui, et le repo local est préparé en 0.6.39 ;
  • le plugin WordPress est actif en 0.1.23 sur ooblik.com ;
  • le release flow plugin est maintenant exécutable et bloqué les oublis.
  • un nouveau lot local 0.6.40 / 0.1.24 est en cours pour aligner les quantités WooCommerce sur les quantités KEREDIT.

La suite logique est de reprendre le parcours client complet en live : produit WooCommerce, création, édition, sauvegarde, commande, retour commande, support backoffice et correction projet.

Il faudra aussi choisir si on termine et publie d’abord le correctif quantités 0.6.40 / 0.1.24, puis si on redeploie le VPS pour un test contrôle sur le produit test-krampouz.

Et surtout : demain, repartir avec la fatigue en moins. Aujourd’hui, il faisait environ 30 degrés dehors et la journée a été longue.

description.source: Journée dense avant bêta : merge du P1 backend, socle Better Auth et Google OAuth, admin utilisateurs robuste, pont WooCommerce vers KEREDIT, checkout éditeur, deploy VPS et verrouillage de la release plugin WordPress.

title.source: Jour 67 - Auth, commerce et procédure qui devient exécutable

items.title: Jour 67 - Auth, commerce et procédure qui devient exécutable

body.source:
Horaires de session

  • Agent utilisé : Codex
  • Date : lundi 25 mai 2026
  • Branche : refactor/admin-pricing-workshop-attributes
  • Version repo : 0.6.29
  • Amplitude observée par les commits : 12:07 -> 16:28, soit 4 h 21 minimum
  • Temps actif estime : environ 4 h 45 a 5 h 30, en comptant les lectures d’audit, validations, rapport HTML et reprises de contexte
  • Commits pousses :
    • 9ad14b0 - refactor: split admin pricing route domains
    • 6c896f6 - refactor: split asset helpers from runtime deps
    • 9bfd0ca - refactor: centralize print job queue workflow
  • Volume visible sur ces commits : 3266 insertions, 1821 suppressions sur les trois lots La journée a continue le chantier commence la veille : remettre le backend KEREDIT dans une architecture lisible, sans repartir dans une vague de refactorisation abstraite. Le fil directeur était simple : une route doit rester un controleur HTTP. Les décisions métier, Prisma, les effets de bord et les queues doivent vivre dans des services nommes, testables, et stables. Hier, ce principe a été applique sur trois points P1.
  • Temps cumulé minimal depuis le début du journal : environ 343h57+

Admin pricing : la route géante devient un assemblage

Le plus gros gain visuel de la journée est sur backend/src/routes/admin/pricing.ts.

Au départ du P1, cette route faisait 2598 lignes avec 128 accès prisma.*. Elle mélangeait trop de domaines : attributs atelier, papiers, matrices, liaisons produit, simulation, MISKISS, overview.
